title: Political Philosophy
topics: Can liberty and equality be reconciled?
Critiques via class, gender and race

notes.body:
Political philosophers disagree about what liberty is, why it matters and how to weigh it when liberties, or liberty and other values, conflict.

Concepts
- Berlin ('Two Concepts of Liberty', 1958): negative liberty is the area in which one is not interfered with by others ('freedom from'); positive liberty is self-mastery ('freedom to'). His worry is that positive liberty splits the self into a 'higher' rational self and a 'lower' empirical one, so rulers can coerce people in the name of their real freedom. Rousseau's 'forced to be free' is a key example.
- MacCallum (1967): every freedom claim is triadic (x is free from y to do or become z), so the debate concerns how to fill in the variables, not two concepts.
- Taylor (1979): negative liberty is an opportunity concept, positive an exercise concept; judging the significance of freedoms pushes us towards the latter.
- Republicans (Pettit, Skinner): freedom as non-domination. The slave of a benevolent master is unfree because he lives under another's arbitrary power.
- Pure negative liberty (Steiner, Carter): one is unfree to do something only if another makes it impossible; threats change the costs of options rather than removing freedom.
- Moralised definitions count only unjust interference. Cohen argued libertarians tacitly rely on one when they say enforcing property rights restricts no one's freedom.
- Internal constraints: positive theorists say addiction or false consciousness can make one unfree; critics reply this blurs freedom with rationality or virtue.

Value and conflict
- Liberty may be valued intrinsically, or instrumentally for happiness, truth, progress or individuality.
- Berlin's value pluralism: values are many and sometimes incompatible, so choosing between them involves real loss.
- Constant (1819): liberty of the ancients (participation) versus the moderns (private independence).
- Liberties collide with each other (expression versus privacy), so any scheme must regulate them.
- Paternalism (Gerald Dworkin, 1972) interferes for a person's own good. Soft paternalism acts only when a choice is not informed or voluntary (Mill's unsafe bridge); hard paternalism overrides informed, voluntary choice. Mill refused to enforce self-enslavement contracts, since freedom cannot require being free not to be free.

Applied example
'Your money or your life': on a pure negative view you could still refuse, at great cost; on a moralised view the robber's unjust threat reduces your freedom; on a republican view you are unfree because you are subject to his arbitrary will.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying Berlin rejected positive liberty outright; he warned about its abuse.
- Assuming republican freedom is just positive liberty.
- Calling a sugar tax hard paternalism without asking whether it removes options or only raises their cost.

Egalitarians disagree about why equality matters, what should be equalised (the 'currency'), and whether equality, priority or sufficiency is the right ideal.

Opportunity and formal equality
- Formal equality (the Aristotelian principle): treat like cases alike; it does not say which differences are relevant.
- Formal equality of opportunity means careers open to talents. Rawls's fair equality of opportunity requires similar life chances for people with similar talent and willingness to use it, whatever their class, which demands active measures such as education.
- Michael Young coined 'meritocracy' (1958) as a satirical warning; it is now often used approvingly.

Currencies and luck
- Luck egalitarianism (Dworkin, Arneson, Cohen): inequalities from brute luck are unjust, those from responsible choice may be fair.
- Dworkin ('Equality of Resources', 1981): brute versus option luck; a clamshell auction that passes the envy test; hypothetical insurance against unequal talents and handicaps. Expensive tastes tell against equality of welfare.
- Arneson (1989): equal opportunity for welfare; Cohen (1989): equal access to advantage.
- Sen ('Equality of What?', 1979): capabilities, because people convert resources into functionings at different rates.

Equality, priority, sufficiency
- Parfit's levelling down objection: if inequality is bad in itself, making the better-off worse off with no gain to anyone would be better in one respect. It mainly threatens telic egalitarianism; deontic egalitarians object only to inequality produced by unfair treatment.
- Prioritarianism: benefits matter more the worse off the recipient is, in absolute terms.
- Sufficientarianism (Frankfurt, 1987): what matters is that everyone has enough.
- Relational equality (Anderson, 1999): end oppression and relate as equals. Luck egalitarianism is harsh to the imprudent (the uninsured negligent driver) and demeaning to the unlucky.
- Walzer (Spheres of Justice, 1983): complex equality; injustice is when advantage in one sphere dominates another.

Political equality
Equal standing in collective decisions. Rawls guarantees the fair value of the political liberties so wealth cannot buy disproportionate influence. Mill (1861) backed a wide suffrage including women but proposed plural votes for the educated. The dictum that everybody counts for one, which Mill attributes to Bentham, expresses utilitarianism's egalitarian element.

Worked example
Three equal groups: P = 30, 30, 30; Q = 35, 50, 80; R = 25, 70, 150. A strict egalitarian prefers P; maximin prefers Q (worst-off 35); a utilitarian prefers R (total 245 against 165 and 90). A prioritarian's choice between Q and R depends on how much extra weight the worst-off receive.

Exam pitfalls
- Conflating prioritarianism with egalitarianism.
- Saying a Gini of 1 means perfect equality; 0 does.
- Treating luck egalitarianism as a single view when its currencies differ.

notes.h: Can liberty and equality be reconciled?
notes.body:
The conflict thesis says more equality requires less liberty. Others argue the conflict disappears, or shrinks, once the concepts are properly understood.

The case for conflict
- Nozick: 'liberty upsets patterns'. Free exchanges (Wilt Chamberlain) disrupt any patterned distribution, so keeping it requires continual interference; a socialist society would have to forbid capitalist acts between consenting adults. Taxation of earnings is 'on a par with forced labor'.
- Hayek (The Constitution of Liberty, 1960): equality before the law fits freedom, but because people differ, making them materially equal means treating them unequally. Later (Law, Legislation and Liberty, vol. 2, 1976) he called social justice a mirage.
- Berlin: liberty is liberty, not equality or fairness. Redistribution may be justified, but we should admit it costs some liberty rather than redefine liberty.

Reconciling strategies
- Rawls: equal basic liberties are lexically prior and may be limited only for liberty's sake. Poverty reduces the worth of liberty, not liberty itself; the difference principle maximises its worth to the least advantaged, and the fair value of political liberties is guaranteed. In Justice as Fairness (2001) he favoured property-owning democracy over welfare-state capitalism.
- Hart (1973) asked why rational parties would always prefer liberty to material gains; Rawls revised his account.
- Cohen ('Freedom and Money'): money works like a ticket; without it you will be physically stopped, so redistributing money redistributes freedom.
- Cohen's incentives critique: if the talented demand higher pay to work harder, inequality is 'necessary' only because of their choices, like a kidnapper's demand that cannot be justified face to face to the poor. An egalitarian ethos needs no coercion, which answers Rawls's worry about occupational freedom.
- Dworkin (Sovereign Virtue, 2000): equal concern is the sovereign virtue, and properly understood the two values cannot genuinely conflict.
- Left-libertarians (Steiner, Otsuka, Vallentyne): full self-ownership plus egalitarian ownership of natural resources supports substantial redistribution.
- Republicans: non-domination requires material independence; Pettit's eyeball test.

Applied example
A cap on political donations restricts a wealthy donor's liberty to spend, but on Rawls's view secures the fair value of political liberty for everyone else. A basic income funded by high taxes limits some property liberty yet, on Cohen's argument, extends the freedom of people without money. Abolishing fee-paying schools sets parents' liberty against fair equality of opportunity.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating reconciliation as proof that no trade-off ever exists; many accounts rank or redefine values instead.
- Missing the moralised-definition point: Nozick's claims depend on prior entitlements.
- Forgetting that Rawls's priority covers the basic liberties, not economic liberty in general.

These five thinkers shaped modern debates about authority, rights, utility and individual freedom.

Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651)
- The state of nature is a war of every man against every man, driven by competition, diffidence and glory under rough equality.
- First law of nature: seek peace where possible, otherwise use the advantages of war. Second: lay down the right to all things when others will too.
- The sovereign, authorised by mutual covenant, must be absolute and undivided because 'covenants, without the sword, are but words'. Subjects keep the right to defend their lives; their liberty lies where the law is silent. Liberty is the absence of external impediments, and fear is consistent with it.

Locke (Second Treatise, 1689)
- The state of nature is governed by a law of nature forbidding harm to life, health, liberty or possessions; its defect is the lack of an impartial judge.
- Property comes from mixing labour with unowned things, subject to the sufficiency ('enough, and as good') and spoilage provisos; money allows accumulation beyond spoilage.
- Express and tacit consent; government is a trust, and breach of trust justifies resistance.

Wollstonecraft (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792)
Women are rational beings whose apparent inferiority stems from an education designed to please men; she answers Rousseau's Emile. Dependence corrupts both sexes, and she wanted women to have power over themselves rather than over men.

Bentham
- The principle of utility (An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation, 1789): judge actions and laws by their tendency to promote happiness.
- The felicific calculus: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent.
- Natural rights are 'nonsense upon stilts'; rights are created by law.

Mill
- Harm principle (On Liberty, 1859): power over a member of a civilised community is justified only to prevent harm to others.
- Free expression: a silenced opinion may be true or partly true, and unchallenged truth becomes dead dogma.
- Individuality and 'experiments of living' against the tyranny of custom.
- Higher and lower pleasures, ranked by competent judges.
- The Subjection of Women (1869): women's legal subordination is wrong and blocks improvement.

Applied example
A blogger spreading vaccine misinformation is protected by Mill's arguments for free expression, but a speaker rousing an angry crowd outside someone's home resembles Mill's own corn-dealer example, where speech becomes a positive instigation to harm.

Exam pitfalls
- Reading Locke's state of nature as Hobbes's war.
- Treating Mill as a simple act-utilitarian; he grounds liberty in utility 'in the largest sense'.
- Presenting Wollstonecraft as merely applying liberal principles; consider her critique of dependence.
- Forgetting that tacit consent risks becoming impossible to withhold.

Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971) and Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) frame the modern liberal debate on distributive justice.

Rawls
- The subject of justice is the basic structure: how major institutions distribute rights, duties and the benefits of cooperation.
- Method: reflective equilibrium between considered judgements and principles.
- Original position: free and equal parties behind a veil of ignorance about class, talents, sex, race, conception of the good and generation, though they know general facts of economics and psychology. They choose over primary goods: rights and liberties, opportunities and powers, income and wealth, and the social bases of self-respect.
- Two principles: equal basic liberties; inequalities attached to positions open under fair equality of opportunity and to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. Liberty is lexically prior, and fair opportunity precedes the difference principle.
- Maximin is rational when probabilities cannot be estimated, gains above a guaranteed minimum matter little, and alternatives risk unacceptable outcomes. Harsanyi argued for equal probabilities and maximising average utility.
- Utilitarianism ignores the separateness of persons. Natural talents are morally arbitrary, and the difference principle treats their distribution as a common asset.
- Political Liberalism (1993): an overlapping consensus among reasonable comprehensive doctrines.

Nozick
- Rights are side constraints, expressing the Kantian idea that persons are ends, not means.
- Entitlement theory: justice in acquisition, transfer and rectification; historical and unpatterned.
- Wilt Chamberlain: from a just D1, a million fans each paying 25 cents gives Chamberlain $250,000; if every transfer was voluntary, how can D2 be unjust?
- Only a minimal state is justified. Nozick charges that Rawls treats goods as 'manna from heaven'.
- His weakened Lockean proviso forbids appropriation only if it leaves others worse off than an unowned baseline; Cohen found this baseline too weak. The tomato juice example questions labour-mixing.

Cohen's critique of Rawls
Incentive-driven inequality depends on the talented's own choices, like a kidnapper's demand; justice requires an egalitarian ethos, not just just institutions. Rawlsians reply that principles of justice apply to the basic structure.

Worked example
Schemes X (30, 40, 50), Y (20, 60, 100), Z (5, 80, 200). Maximin picks X (worst-off 30). Harsanyi picks Z (average 95 against 60 and 40). A Rawlsian adds that Z's minimum of 5 risks an outcome one could hardly accept.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying parties know nothing; they know general social facts.
- Treating Wilt as decisive without replies: effects on third parties, and whether D1 entitlements already include full rights to all income.
- Equating the difference principle with maximin as a general decision rule.

notes.h: Critiques via class, gender and race
notes.body:
Critics argue that liberal theories of liberty, equality and contract abstract from, and can conceal, domination by class, gender and race.

Class
- Marx ('On the Jewish Question', 1843): political emancipation (equal rights, a secular state) leaves civil society's egoism and inequality intact; human emancipation requires transforming social life.
- The worker is 'free' in a double sense: legally free to sell labour power, and free of any means of production, so compelled to sell it (Capital, 1867).
- Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875): equal right is a right of inequality because people differ; a higher phase follows 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'.
- Base and superstructure: liberal ideals may legitimise capitalist relations.

Gender
- Okin (Justice, Gender, and the Family, 1989): Rawls assumed the family just and treated the parties as heads of families, yet the gendered family belongs to the basic structure, makes women vulnerable and is the first school of moral development.
- Pateman (The Sexual Contract, 1988): the social contract conceals a prior sexual contract establishing men's political right over women.
- 'The personal is political' challenges the liberal public/private divide.
- MacKinnon's dominance approach: the issue is hierarchy, not sameness or difference.

Race
- Charles Mills (The Racial Contract, 1997): the real contract was among whites, classing non-whites as subpersons and sustained by an epistemology of ignorance. 'Ideal Theory as Ideology' (2005): idealisation abstracts from oppression and serves the privileged; he sought to reclaim liberalism through non-ideal theory.
- Locke's treatment of uncultivated land as waste was used to deny Indigenous ownership, and he was involved in administering the Carolina colony. Mill limited the harm principle to people in the maturity of their faculties, accepted despotism over 'barbarians' aimed at improvement, and worked for the East India Company.

Structural and plural accounts
- Young (1990): five faces of oppression, criticising the distributive paradigm.
- Crenshaw (1989): intersectionality.
- Fraser: redistribution and recognition are distinct dimensions of justice.
- Ideal theory assumes full compliance; non-ideal theory starts from actual injustice.

Applied illustration
A Rawlsian asks what principles free and equal parties would choose; Okin asks who does the unpaid care in families; Mills asks how present wealth gaps trace back to racial expropriation that ideal theory sets aside.

Exam pitfalls
- Assuming all critics reject liberalism; Okin and Mills aim to reform it.
- Equating Pateman and Mills: Pateman treats contract itself as a vehicle of subordination, Mills a corrupted but redeemable ideal.
- Using intersectionality as a label without showing how combined categories change the analysis.
- Ignoring defenders of contract theory, who argue its ideals can be turned against exclusion.

cards.b: Freedom as the absence of interference: the area within which a person can act without being obstructed by other people. Berlin's 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958) calls it 'freedom from'.
Freedom as self-mastery or self-government: being the author of one's own choices, ruled by one's own reason rather than by others or by one's passions. Often glossed as 'freedom to'.

Gerald MacCallum (1967) argued that every freedom claim has the form 'x is free from y to do or become z'. On his view the negative/positive debate is a disagreement about what counts as the agent, the constraint and the goal, not a clash between two concepts.

Associated with Philip Pettit and Quentin Skinner: you are unfree if another can interfere arbitrarily in your choices, even if they never actually do. Depending on another's goodwill is itself a loss of freedom.

A slave whose kind master never interferes suffers little actual interference, so a pure non-interference view struggles to call him unfree. Republicans use the case to show that domination, not interference, is what makes the slave unfree.

cards.f: Berlin's main worry about positive liberty
cards.b: It invites splitting the self into a 'higher' rational self and a 'lower' empirical self. Rulers who claim to know the higher self can then coerce people in the name of their 'real' freedom.

In The Social Contract (1762) Rousseau says that whoever refuses to obey the general will may be compelled to obey it, which means only that he will be 'forced to be free'. Berlin treats this as a paradigm of the dangers of positive liberty.

Ultimate human values are many, genuinely different and sometimes incompatible, so no political order can realise all of them and choosing between them involves real loss. Berlin thought this supports negative liberty as protecting room for choice.

cards.f: Taylor: opportunity vs exercise concepts of freedom
cards.b: In 'What's Wrong with Negative Liberty' (1979) Charles Taylor called negative liberty an opportunity concept (having options open) and positive liberty an exercise concept (actually directing one's life). He argued we must judge the significance of freedoms, which pushes us towards the exercise concept.

The view that a person is unfree to do something only if another person makes it impossible for them to do it. On this view threats and offers do not strictly remove freedom; they change the costs of options.

cards.f: Moralised vs non-moralised definitions of freedom
cards.b: A moralised definition counts only unjust or illegitimate interference as reducing freedom; a non-moralised one counts any interference. G.A. Cohen argued that libertarians rely on a moralised definition when they say enforcing property rights does not restrict anyone's freedom.
Interfering with a person's liberty against their will, justified by the claim that it is for their own good (Gerald Dworkin, 'Paternalism', 1972).

Soft paternalism intervenes only when a choice is not fully informed or voluntary, to check what the person really wants; hard paternalism overrides choices that are informed and voluntary. Mill's unsafe bridge example is usually read as soft paternalism.

cards.f: Intrinsic vs instrumental value of liberty
cards.b: Liberty may be valued for its own sake, as part of a dignified or self-directed life, or for what it produces, such as happiness, the discovery of truth, progress or the development of individuality.

cards.f: Constant: the liberty of the ancients vs the moderns
cards.b: Benjamin Constant (1819) contrasted ancient liberty, active collective share in sovereignty, with modern liberty, the peaceful enjoyment of private independence. He warned against sacrificing modern liberty to the ancient kind.

Liberties can collide with each other, not only with other values: for example one person's freedom of expression against another's privacy or freedom of association. Any workable scheme of liberties has to regulate and limit particular liberties.

Positive-liberty theorists hold that addiction, compulsion, ignorance or false consciousness can make a person unfree without any external interference. Critics reply that this blurs freedom into rationality or virtue.

cards.f: Mill on selling oneself into slavery
cards.b: Mill held that a contract to sell oneself into slavery should not be enforced: by alienating his liberty the person defeats the very purpose of allowing him to choose, and the principle of freedom cannot require that he be 'free not to be free'.
Careers open to talents: positions are open to all and allocated without legal or discriminatory barriers. Social background may still shape who is able to compete successfully.

Those with similar talent and similar willingness to use it should have similar life chances, whatever class they were born into. It requires active measures, such as education, to counter social disadvantage.
Treat like cases alike and unlike cases differently, in proportion to the relevant differences. It is formal because it does not say which differences are relevant.
A summary measure of income or wealth inequality derived from the Lorenz curve: 0 means perfect equality (everyone has the same) and 1 means one person has everything.

The view that inequalities arising from brute luck (unchosen circumstances) are unjust, while those resulting from people's responsible choices may be fair. Associated with Dworkin, Arneson and G.A. Cohen.

Option luck is how deliberate, calculated gambles turn out; brute luck is how risks fall that were not deliberately taken, such as being born with a disability. Dworkin draws the distinction in 'Equality of Resources' (1981).

cards.f: Dworkin's auction and the envy test
cards.b: Shipwrecked immigrants bid for all the island's resources using equal numbers of clamshells; the outcome is equal if no one prefers anyone else's bundle to their own (the envy test). A hypothetical insurance market then addresses unequal brute luck in talents and handicaps.

Equality of welfare seems to require giving more resources to someone who has cultivated costly tastes (Dworkin's example involves plovers' eggs and pre-phylloxera claret). This looks unfair to people with cheap tastes and motivates resource-based views.
Benefits matter more the worse off the person receiving them is. Unlike egalitarianism, it is concerned with people's absolute levels of wellbeing, not with how they compare with one another.

If inequality is bad in itself, then making the better off worse off, with no gain to anyone, would be better in at least one respect. Parfit argued in 'Equality or Priority?' that many find this absurd, which pushes them towards prioritarianism.

Telic egalitarians think inequality is bad as a state of affairs; deontic egalitarians think it is objectionable only when it results from wrongdoing or unfair treatment by some agent. Deontic views escape the levelling down objection more easily.

Harry Frankfurt's 'Equality as a Moral Ideal' (1987) argued that what matters morally is that everyone has enough, not that everyone has the same. Inequalities above the threshold are not themselves objectionable.

Elizabeth Anderson's 'What Is the Point of Equality?' (1999) holds that equality is about ending oppression and relating to one another as equals, not compensating bad luck. She criticises luck egalitarianism as harsh to the imprudent and demeaning to the unlucky.

Sen's 1979 Tanner lecture 'Equality of What?' proposed focusing on capabilities, the real freedoms people have to achieve valuable functionings. Equal resources can leave people unequal because they convert resources into functionings at different rates, for example a disabled person.

cards.f: Equal opportunity for welfare and equal access to advantage
cards.b: Richard Arneson (1989) defended equal opportunity for welfare; G.A. Cohen (1989) defended equal access to advantage, a broader currency covering both welfare and resources. Both build personal responsibility into egalitarianism.

Each citizen has equal standing in collective decisions: one person, one vote, and arguably a fair chance to influence outcomes. Rawls requires the 'fair value' of the political liberties to be guaranteed, so that wealth cannot buy disproportionate political power.

In Considerations on Representative Government (1861) Mill supported a very wide suffrage, including women, but proposed extra votes for the better educated, a deliberate departure from strict political equality.

Young coined the term in The Rise of the Meritocracy (1958), a satire warning that a society ranking people by measured merit could be harsh and self-justifying. It is now often used approvingly, reversing his intent.

In Spheres of Justice (1983) Michael Walzer argued that each social good has its own sphere and distributive principle; injustice arises when advantage in one sphere, such as money, comes to dominate others, such as political office or healthcare.

cards.f: 'Everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one'
cards.b: A dictum Mill attributes to Bentham in Utilitarianism. It expresses utilitarianism's egalitarian element: equal interests count equally, whoever has them, though it does not require equal outcomes.
The claim that liberty and equality necessarily trade off: securing more equal outcomes requires restricting people's freedom to use, exchange and keep what they have.
Nozick's slogan: any patterned distribution will be disrupted by people's free exchanges, so maintaining it requires continual interference with their choices.
Nozick claimed that 'Taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor': taking the earnings of n hours' work is like forcing someone to work n hours for another's purposes.
Nozick argued that a socialist society 'would have to forbid capitalist acts between consenting adults', to show that equality must be enforced against free exchange.

cards.f: Berlin on conflating liberty with other values
cards.b: Berlin insisted that 'liberty is liberty, not equality or fairness or justice'. Redistribution may be justified, but we should say honestly that it trades away some liberty rather than redefine liberty.

The first principle (equal basic liberties) has strict priority over the second: basic liberties may be limited only for the sake of liberty itself, not traded for economic or social gains, at least once reasonably favourable conditions obtain.

cards.f: Liberty vs the worth of liberty (Rawls)
cards.b: For Rawls poverty does not reduce a person's basic liberties but reduces their worth, i.e. the ability to make use of them. The difference principle maximises the worth of liberty to the least advantaged, and the fair value of the political liberties is guaranteed for all.

G.A. Cohen argued that money works like a ticket: someone without a fare who boards a train will be physically removed. Since lacking money exposes you to interference, redistributing money redistributes freedom, so equality can increase liberty.

cards.f: Dworkin: equality as the sovereign virtue
cards.b: In Sovereign Virtue (2000) Dworkin argued that equal concern is the sovereign political virtue and that, once liberty and equality are properly understood, they cannot genuinely conflict.

cards.f: Hayek: equality before the law vs material equality
cards.b: Hayek (The Constitution of Liberty, 1960) held that equality before the law fits with freedom, but since people differ, making them materially equal requires treating them unequally and so restricts liberty. He later called 'social justice' a mirage in Law, Legislation and Liberty, vol. 2: The Mirage of Social Justice (1976).

Combines full self-ownership with egalitarian ownership of natural resources (e.g. Hillel Steiner, Michael Otsuka, Peter Vallentyne). Those who appropriate more than their share of the world owe the rest, offering a libertarian route to substantial redistribution.

If freedom is non-domination, people who depend on employers, spouses or officials for subsistence are unfree, so securing freedom requires some material independence and equality. Pettit's 'eyeball test' asks whether citizens can look one another in the eye without fear or deference.

In Why Not Socialism? (2009) Cohen imagined a camping trip on which people share equipment and cooperate freely, arguing that most would find market-style bargaining there objectionable. He used it to suggest that equality and community need not feel coercive.

In Justice as Fairness: A Restatement (2001) Rawls argued that welfare-state capitalism cannot realise his principles, and favoured a property-owning democracy that disperses ownership of wealth and capital in advance rather than redistributing after the fact.

cards.f: Hart on Rawls's priority of liberty
cards.b: H.L.A. Hart (1973) argued that Rawls gave no convincing reason why rational parties would always prefer liberty to material gains, and that conflicts between basic liberties cannot be settled by appeal to liberty alone. Rawls later revised his account in response.

cards.f: Occupational freedom and the egalitarian ethos
cards.b: Rawls held that forcing talented people into their most productive jobs would violate freedom of occupation. Cohen replied that an egalitarian ethos, under which people choose to work for less, asks for no coercion, so equality need not cost that liberty.
In Leviathan (1651), without a common power people are in a war of every man against every man, and life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'.
Competition (for gain), diffidence (distrust, seeking safety) and glory (reputation). Because people are roughly equal and anyone can kill anyone, pre-emptive attack becomes rational.

cards.f: Hobbes's first and second laws of nature
cards.b: First: seek peace where it can be had, and otherwise use all the advantages of war. Second: be willing, when others are too, to lay down the right to all things and be content with as much liberty against others as you would allow them against yourself.

Created when each person covenants with every other to authorise one person or assembly; its power is absolute and undivided, because 'covenants, without the sword, are but words'. Subjects keep only the right to defend their own lives.
Liberty is the absence of external impediments to motion. Acting from fear is still acting freely ('fear and liberty are consistent'), and the liberty of subjects lies where the law is silent.

In the Second Treatise (1689) the state of nature is governed by a law of nature, known by reason, forbidding harm to others in their life, health, liberty or possessions. Its defect is the lack of an impartial judge and enforcer.
Each person owns their own person and labour; by mixing their labour with unowned natural resources they make those resources their property.

Appropriation is legitimate only if 'enough, and as good' is left in common for others (the sufficiency proviso) and nothing is taken that will spoil unused (the spoilage proviso). The invention of money lets people accumulate beyond the spoilage limit.

cards.f: Locke on express and tacit consent
cards.b: Express consent makes one a full member of society; tacit consent is given by enjoying property or protection, even by travelling freely on the highway. Critics say this makes consent so easy to give that it loses its legitimising force.
Government holds power on trust to protect life, liberty and estate; when rulers act contrary to that trust, the people may resist and set up a new government.

cards.f: Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792)
cards.b: Argues that women are rational beings whose apparent inferiority comes from a lack of education and from being trained to please men. It replies directly to Rousseau's account of women's education in Emile.
She argued that dependence on men's favour corrupts both sexes and makes genuine virtue impossible for women. Of women she wrote: 'I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.'

Actions and laws should be judged by their tendency to increase or diminish happiness, understood as pleasure and the absence of pain. Set out in An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789).

cards.f: Bentham: natural rights as 'nonsense upon stilts'
cards.b: Bentham rejected natural and imprescriptible rights as rhetorical nonsense; for him rights are created by law and must be justified by their utility.
A method for measuring pleasures and pains by their intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity, purity and extent (the number of people affected).

In On Liberty (1859) Mill holds that the only legitimate reason for exercising power over a member of a civilised community against his will is 'to prevent harm to others'. His own good is not a sufficient warrant.

Conduct that affects only the agent, or others only with their free consent, is self-regarding and outside society's control; conduct that harms others' interests may be regulated. 'Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.'

Silencing an opinion is wrong because it may be true; even if false it may contain part of the truth; even a true view held without challenge becomes 'dead dogma'; and its meaning and effect on conduct may be lost.

cards.f: Mill on individuality and social tyranny
cards.b: Mill feared the pressure of custom and majority opinion more than law, and valued 'experiments of living' through which individuals develop their faculties and society discovers better ways to live.

Some pleasures, of the intellect, feelings and imagination, are of higher quality, as shown by the preference of competent judges who have experienced both; it is 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'.

Argues that the legal subordination of women, especially in marriage, is wrong in itself and a major obstacle to human improvement, and that women's 'nature' cannot be known while it is shaped by subordination.

cards.f: The original position and the veil of ignorance
cards.b: Rawls's device for choosing principles of justice: free and equal parties choose without knowing their class, talents, sex, race, conception of the good or generation, so that the principles cannot be tailored to their own advantage.

First, equal basic liberties for all. Second, social and economic inequalities must be attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and be to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle).
Social and economic inequalities are just only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society, compared with the feasible alternatives.

Things any rational person is presumed to want, whatever else they want: rights and liberties, opportunities and powers, income and wealth, and the social bases of self-respect. They are the currency of Rawlsian justice.

For Rawls the primary subject of justice is the way the major social institutions (constitution, economy, property system, family) distribute fundamental rights and duties and the benefits of social cooperation.
Rawls's method of moving back and forth between considered judgements about particular cases and general principles, revising each until they cohere.

cards.f: Rawls's separateness of persons objection to utilitarianism
cards.b: Utilitarianism extends the principle of rational choice for one person to society as a whole, treating losses to some as made up by gains to others; in doing so it does not take seriously the distinction between persons.

cards.f: Maximin and Rawls's conditions for using it
cards.b: Maximin ranks options by their worst outcomes. Rawls said it is rational when probabilities cannot be reliably estimated, the chooser cares little about gains above a guaranteed minimum, and the alternatives risk outcomes one could hardly accept.
John Harsanyi argued that rational choosers behind a veil should assign equal probability to occupying each position and maximise expected, i.e. average, utility; maximin is irrationally risk-averse.

The natural distribution of talents is morally arbitrary, 'neither just nor unjust'; what matters is how institutions deal with it. The difference principle in effect treats the distribution of natural talents as a common asset.

Rawls recast justice as fairness as a political conception that citizens holding different reasonable comprehensive doctrines could endorse through an overlapping consensus, given the fact of reasonable pluralism.

A distribution is just if everyone is entitled to what they hold under three principles: justice in acquisition, justice in transfer, and rectification of past injustice (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974).

cards.f: Historical vs end-state and patterned principles
cards.b: Historical principles judge distributions by how they came about; end-state principles by the structure of the result. Patterned principles distribute according to some natural dimension ('to each according to his...'). Nozick's theory is historical and unpatterned.

Start from any just distribution D1. Chamberlain's contract gives him 25 cents of each ticket price; over a season a million fans freely pay to watch him, and he ends up with $250,000. If D1 was just and every transfer was voluntary, how can the new distribution D2 be unjust?

Rights act as constraints on what anyone may do to others, not as goals to be maximised. They express the Kantian idea that individuals are ends and not merely means, and may not be sacrificed for others without consent.

A night-watchman state limited to protection against force, theft and fraud and the enforcement of contracts. Nozick argued it could arise from anarchy without violating rights, via a dominant protective agency, but any more extensive state violates rights.

cards.f: Nozick's version of the Lockean proviso
cards.b: An appropriation is legitimate unless it makes others worse off than they would be in a baseline where the thing stayed unowned. Critics such as Cohen argue this baseline is far too weak.

cards.f: Nozick's tomato juice objection to Locke
cards.b: If I pour my can of tomato juice into the sea, do I come to own the sea or simply lose my juice? Nozick used this to show that 'mixing labour' cannot by itself explain how acquisition works.

If talented people will produce more only for higher pay, the resulting inequality is 'necessary' only because of their own choices. Like a kidnapper's demand, this cannot be justified face to face to the poor; a just society needs an egalitarian ethos, not only just institutions.
Rawls's original position treats goods as if they fell from heaven unowned and ready to be distributed, ignoring that they are produced by people who may already have entitlements to them.

In 'On the Jewish Question' (1843) Marx argued that political emancipation, equal rights and a state freed from religion, leaves the egoism and inequality of civil society intact; full human emancipation requires transforming social life itself.
In Capital (1867) the worker is free in a double sense: legally free to sell his labour power, and 'free' of any means of production, so in practice compelled to sell it.

Marx argued that equal right in the first phase of communism is still a right of inequality, because people differ; a higher phase would follow 'From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs!'
Marx's claim that a society's economic structure shapes its legal, political and ideological forms, so liberal ideals of liberty and equality may serve to legitimise capitalist class relations.

cards.f: Okin: Justice, Gender, and the Family (1989)
cards.b: Susan Moller Okin argued that Rawls assumed the family was just and treated the parties as heads of families, yet the gendered family is part of the basic structure, makes women vulnerable and is the first school of moral development.

Carole Pateman argued that the social contract story hides a prior sexual contract that established men's political right over women, so contract has been a vehicle of patriarchal subordination rather than freedom.

A second-wave feminist slogan holding that relations in the home, sexuality and the family are structured by power and are proper subjects of justice, challenging the liberal divide between public and private.

cards.f: Iris Marion Young's five faces of oppression
cards.b: Exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence (Justice and the Politics of Difference, 1990). Young criticised the 'distributive paradigm' for neglecting social structures and relations.
Catharine MacKinnon argued that asking whether women are the same as or different from men misses the point: gender is a hierarchy of power, so the real issue is male dominance, not difference.

Mills argued that the actual contract underpinning modern Western politics was a racial one among whites, which classed non-whites as subpersons, and that it was sustained by an 'epistemology of ignorance'.

Mills argued that ideal theory abstracts away from oppression and idealises agents and institutions, and so tends to serve the privileged. He favoured non-ideal theory starting from actual injustice, while still seeking to reclaim liberalism rather than abandon it.

Kimberlé Crenshaw's term (1989) for the way race, gender and other categories interact, so that, for example, Black women can face discrimination that neither a race-only nor a sex-only analysis captures.

Locke's treatment of uncultivated land as 'waste', and his remark that 'in the beginning all the world was America', were used to deny that Indigenous peoples owned land they hunted rather than farmed. Locke was also involved in the administration of the Carolina colony, whose Fundamental Constitutions (1669) sanctioned slavery.

Mill restricted the harm principle to people 'in the maturity of their faculties' and wrote that despotism is a legitimate way of governing 'barbarians' if it aims at their improvement. He worked for the East India Company for over three decades.
Ideal theory asks what a perfectly just society would look like, assuming full compliance with its principles; non-ideal theory asks how to respond to actual injustice and partial compliance.

Nancy Fraser argued that justice has at least two dimensions: redistribution, to address class-like economic injustice, and recognition, to address status injustice such as racism and sexism; neither reduces to the other.

questions.q: Which of the following best captures Isaiah Berlin's idea of negative liberty?
options: The absence of interference by other people within an area of action
Having a share in collective self-government
Being ruled by one's rational or 'higher' self
Possessing the resources needed to achieve one's goals
questions.why: Berlin defines negative liberty as the area within which one can act unobstructed by others. Self-mastery and self-government belong to positive liberty, and the resources view is closer to Rawls's 'worth of liberty' or Sen's capabilities.

questions.q: Which thinker described life in the state of nature as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'?
options: John Locke
Thomas Hobbes
Jean-Jacques Rousseau
Jeremy Bentham
questions.why: The phrase comes from Hobbes's Leviathan (1651), ch. 13. Locke's state of nature is governed by a law of nature and is far less bleak.

questions.q: A country's income Gini coefficient is reported as 0. What does this mean?
options: One person receives all the income
Inequality is average by international standards
Incomes are perfectly equal
There is no data on income distribution
questions.why: The Gini coefficient runs from 0, where everyone has the same income, to 1, where one person has everything.

questions.q: Who introduced the term 'intersectionality' to describe how race and gender discrimination combine?
options: bell hooks
Angela Davis
Patricia Hill Collins
Kimberlé Crenshaw
questions.why: Crenshaw coined the term in a 1989 article on anti-discrimination law and Black women. The others are important Black feminist thinkers but did not introduce the term.

questions.q: In Rawls's original position, which of the following do the parties know?
options: Their social class
Their conception of the good
General facts about economics and human psychology
Their natural talents and abilities
questions.why: The veil hides particular facts about oneself (class, talents, conception of the good), but the parties know general facts about society, economics and psychology so that they can choose workable principles.

questions.q: According to Rawls, how does poverty relate to liberty?
options: Poverty reduces the worth of liberty, not liberty itself
Poverty is itself a restriction of basic liberty
Poverty is irrelevant to liberty and justice
Poverty justifies limiting the basic liberties of the rich
questions.why: Rawls distinguishes liberty from its worth: the poor have the same basic liberties but less ability to make use of them, which the difference principle addresses.

questions.q: Under Mill's harm principle, which of the following is NOT a legitimate ground for coercing an adult of sound mind?
options: Preventing him from defrauding his neighbours
Preventing him from inciting an angry mob to attack someone
Requiring him to give evidence in court
Preventing him from harming himself when no one else is affected
questions.why: Mill says a person's own good, physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant for coercion. He accepts that people can be compelled to do positive acts such as giving evidence, and that incitement to imminent harm can be restrained.

questions.q: On the republican (neo-Roman) account, why is the slave of a kind master unfree even though the master never interferes?
options: Because the slave lacks material resources
Because the slave lives under another's power of arbitrary interference
Because the slave has not achieved rational self-mastery
Because the slave did not consent to the arrangement
questions.why: For Pettit and Skinner, unfreedom is domination: being subject to another's capacity to interfere at will, whether or not that capacity is used.

questions.q: How should Nozick's entitlement theory of justice be classified?
options: Historical and unpatterned
End-state and patterned
Historical and patterned
End-state and unpatterned
questions.why: Nozick judges holdings by how they arose (acquisition, transfer, rectification), not by the shape of the result, and does not distribute according to any natural dimension such as need or merit.

questions.q: Parfit's levelling down objection is most damaging to which position?
options: Prioritarianism
Sufficientarianism
Telic egalitarianism
Deontic egalitarianism
questions.why: If inequality is bad in itself as a state of affairs (telic egalitarianism), removing it by making the better off worse off must be better in one respect. Prioritarians and sufficientarians do not value equality as such, and deontic views only object to inequality produced by wrongful agency.

questions.q: What is the core claim of G.A. Cohen's argument in 'Freedom and Money'?
options: Money is a resource that has nothing to do with freedom
Markets maximise freedom because they are voluntary
Freedom should be measured by the value of one's property
Lack of money exposes people to interference, so redistributing money redistributes freedom
questions.why: Cohen notes that someone without money who tries to use goods, like a person boarding a train without a ticket, will be stopped. Money therefore removes interference, so it bears directly on negative freedom.

questions.q: What is Susan Moller Okin's central criticism of Rawls in Justice, Gender, and the Family (1989)?
options: Rawls should have abandoned the original position altogether
Rawls assumes the family is just and fails to apply his principles to it, although it is part of the basic structure
Rawls places too much weight on the family as a source of moral development
Rawls's theory is only about race, not gender
questions.why: Okin argues that Rawls takes the family's justice for granted, while the gendered division of labour within it is a central source of women's vulnerability and of children's moral learning, so it must fall under the principles of justice.

questions.q: According to Locke, what allows individuals to accumulate property legitimately beyond what they can use before it spoils?
options: The consent of the sovereign
The labour of servants
The invention of money
The law of nations
questions.why: Money does not spoil, so by agreeing to use it people tacitly consent to unequal holdings that would otherwise breach the spoilage proviso (Second Treatise, ch. 5).

questions.q: Rawls argues that maximin is the rational rule in the original position under certain conditions. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: The parties know that they are, by temperament, unusually averse to risk
The parties care little for gains above the minimum they can guarantee
The rejected alternatives risk outcomes the parties could hardly accept
The parties cannot reliably estimate probabilities of ending up in each position
questions.why: Rawls insists the parties do not know their attitude to risk; maximin is supposed to be rational given the special features of the choice situation, not a matter of the parties' psychology. This is why Harsanyi's charge that it is merely excessive risk-aversion needs answering on other grounds.

questions.q: Elizabeth Anderson's 'What Is the Point of Equality?' (1999) objects to luck egalitarianism partly because it seems to imply that:
options: the state should equalise everyone's welfare regardless of choices
inequality is acceptable as long as everyone has enough
talents should be treated as a common asset
a negligent driver who chose not to insure may be left without urgent medical care
questions.why: Anderson's 'abandonment of negligent victims' charge: if inequalities from choice are not the state's concern, the uninsured careless driver has no claim. She also argues it treats the naturally unlucky with demeaning pity. Treating talents as a common asset is Rawls's idea, and 'enough for everyone' is Frankfurt's sufficientarianism.

questions.q: Distinguish negative from positive liberty as Berlin presents them.
markScheme: Negative liberty: the absence of interference by others; the area in which one can act unobstructed ('freedom from')
Positive liberty: self-mastery or self-government; being the author of one's own life or acting from one's rational self ('freedom to')
questions.modelAnswer: In 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958) Berlin distinguishes two questions. Negative liberty answers 'how far am I left alone?': it is the area within which a person can act without being obstructed by other people. Positive liberty answers 'who governs me?': it is the freedom of self-mastery, being one's own master and directing one's life by one's own reason rather than being driven by others or by one's own passions. Berlin feared that positive liberty, by splitting the self into higher and lower parts, could be used to justify coercion.

questions.q: State the two limits (provisos) that Locke places on acquiring property by labour.
markScheme: Sufficiency proviso: one may appropriate only if 'enough, and as good' is left in common for others
Spoilage proviso: one may not take more than one can use before it spoils or is wasted
questions.modelAnswer: Locke holds that mixing one's labour with unowned resources creates a property right, but subject to two limits. First, the sufficiency proviso: appropriation is legitimate only where enough, and as good, is left in common for others. Second, the spoilage proviso: no one may take more than they can make use of before it spoils, since nothing was made by God for people to waste. Locke later argues that money, which does not spoil, allows people to accumulate beyond this second limit.

questions.q: Distinguish formal equality of opportunity from fair equality of opportunity, illustrating the difference with an example.
markScheme: Formal equality of opportunity: positions open to all, with no legal or discriminatory barriers (careers open to talents)
Fair equality of opportunity (Rawls): people with similar talent and motivation should have similar prospects whatever their social background, requiring active measures such as education
A relevant example showing that formal openness can coexist with unequal prospects (e.g. a university that admits by exam alone while private tuition skews results)
questions.modelAnswer: Formal equality of opportunity requires only that positions be open to everyone and allocated without legal or discriminatory barriers. Fair equality of opportunity, as Rawls defines it, goes further: people with similar natural talents and similar willingness to use them should have similar chances of success regardless of the class into which they were born. For example, a law firm that recruits purely on interview performance satisfies formal equality, yet if candidates from wealthy families have had coaching, networks and better schooling, equally talented poorer candidates still have worse prospects. Fair equality would require measures such as good state education to correct this.

questions.q: State Rawls's two principles of justice and explain how they are ranked.
markScheme: First principle: each person has an equal right to the most extensive (later: a fully adequate) scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with the same for all
Second principle: inequalities must be attached to offices open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and be to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (difference principle)
Lexical priority: the first principle has priority over the second, and fair equality of opportunity has priority over the difference principle
questions.modelAnswer: Rawls's first principle guarantees each person an equal scheme of basic liberties, such as political liberty, freedom of conscience and expression, and the rule of law, compatible with a similar scheme for all. The second principle permits social and economic inequalities only if (a) they are attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity and (b) they are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, the difference principle. The principles are lexically ordered: the basic liberties cannot be traded for economic gains, and fair equality of opportunity takes priority over the difference principle.

questions.q: Outline Mill's arguments in On Liberty, ch. 2, for protecting the expression of opinion, including opinions that are false.
markScheme: The silenced opinion may be true; suppressing it assumes our own infallibility
Even a false opinion may contain part of the truth, which emerges only through collision with other views
Even a wholly true opinion, if never challenged, is held as 'dead dogma' or prejudice, without understanding of its grounds
The meaning of an unchallenged doctrine may be lost or weakened, so it no longer shapes character and conduct
questions.modelAnswer: Mill gives four grounds. First, the silenced opinion may be true, and to suppress it is to assume we are infallible. Second, even an opinion that is mostly wrong may contain a portion of truth, and since prevailing opinion is rarely the whole truth, the missing part can only be supplied by allowing conflicting views. Third, even if received opinion is wholly true, unless it is vigorously contested it will be held as a prejudice, with little grasp of its rational grounds. Fourth, the meaning of the doctrine itself risks being lost, so that it becomes a formal profession with no real effect on character or conduct.

questions.q: Briefly explain Carole Pateman's thesis in The Sexual Contract (1988).
markScheme: Classic contract theory presents society as founded on a free agreement among equals
Pateman argues this story conceals a prior 'sexual contract' establishing men's political right over women (e.g. through the marriage contract)
Contract therefore has been a mechanism of subordination, not simply freedom, so adding women to contract theory is not enough
questions.modelAnswer: Social contract theorists present political society as created by free and equal individuals agreeing to its terms. Pateman argues that this is only half the story: the original pact was also a sexual contract, through which men secured political right over women, most visibly in the marriage contract and the division between public and private spheres. Because the 'individual' of contract theory is implicitly male, contract has served as a vehicle for patriarchal subordination rather than for freedom, so feminists cannot simply extend contract to women without questioning the idea itself.

questions.q: Explain Nozick's claim that 'liberty upsets patterns', and give one reply an egalitarian might make.
markScheme: Patterned principles require a distribution to fit some formula (need, merit, equality)
Free exchanges, gifts and transfers between people will continually disrupt any such pattern (Wilt Chamberlain)
So maintaining a pattern needs continual interference with people's choices, which Nozick sees as violating liberty

A reasonable reply, e.g. Rawls: justice regulates the background institutions (tax rules) so people know their entitlements in advance and are not interfered with transaction by transaction; or Cohen: the transfers affect third parties who did not consent
questions.modelAnswer: Patterned principles say a distribution is just if it matches some formula, such as equality or need. Nozick argues that if people are left free to use their just shares, they will exchange and give in ways that upset any pattern, as when fans pay to watch Wilt Chamberlain. Keeping the pattern would therefore require constantly taking from some and forbidding certain exchanges, which seriously restricts liberty. An egalitarian can reply, following Rawls, that justice applies to the basic structure: stable rules of taxation are announced in advance, so people know what they are entitled to keep and are not interfered with transaction by transaction. Liberty is exercised within just rules rather than upset by them.

questions.q: Explain Gerald MacCallum's triadic analysis of freedom and what it implies for Berlin's distinction between two concepts of liberty.
markScheme: Every freedom claim has the form: agent x is free from constraint y to do or become z
Freedom is a single triadic relation, not two different concepts

Apparent differences between 'negative' and 'positive' theorists reflect disagreement about the range of x, y and z (e.g. whether the agent is the empirical or 'true' self; whether internal obstacles count as constraints)
Implication: the debate should focus on which constraints and agents matter rather than on two rival concepts
questions.modelAnswer: MacCallum argued in 1967 that all talk of freedom has the same structure: an agent (x) is free from some constraint (y) to do or become something (z). Freedom is therefore a single triadic relation. 'Freedom from' and 'freedom to' are not rival concepts but two aspects of the same relation, every freedom being both. On this view Berlin's two camps actually disagree over how to fill in the variables: who counts as the agent (the empirical self or a 'true' rational self), what counts as a constraint (only deliberate human interference, or also poverty, ignorance or compulsion), and which goals matter. The useful questions are about those substantive disagreements.

questions.q: Explain Dworkin's distinction between brute luck and option luck, and how hypothetical insurance is meant to deal with unequal brute luck.
markScheme: Option luck: how deliberate, calculated gambles turn out; the person is responsible for the result
Brute luck: how risks fall that were not deliberate gambles (e.g. congenital disability, being struck by a meteor)
Equality of resources should be sensitive to ambition (choices) but insensitive to endowments (brute luck)
Hypothetical insurance: ask what cover people would buy against handicaps or low talent if all were equally at risk; fund compensation through taxation that mimics those premiums
questions.modelAnswer: Dworkin distinguishes option luck, the outcome of deliberate, calculated gambles such as investing in shares, from brute luck, the way risks fall that were not chosen, such as being born blind. An egalitarian distribution should be 'ambition-sensitive', letting people bear the costs of their choices, but 'endowment-insensitive', not letting unchosen handicaps determine their share. Since the brute luck of disability or low earning power cannot be undone directly, Dworkin asks what insurance people would buy against such risks if they were all equally likely to suffer them. A tax-funded scheme modelled on those hypothetical premiums converts brute luck partly into something like option luck.

questions.q: Explain Harsanyi's objection to the use of maximin in the original position and give one Rawlsian reply.
markScheme: Harsanyi: rational choice under uncertainty should assign equal probability to each position (principle of insufficient reason)
Rational parties would then maximise expected utility, i.e. average utility, leading to utilitarianism
Maximin is irrationally risk-averse: it would forgo large gains for many to avoid small losses for a few

Rawlsian reply, e.g. the stakes are one's whole life and basic liberties, no reliable probabilities exist, the strains of commitment and the need for publicity and stability favour guaranteeing an acceptable minimum
questions.modelAnswer: Harsanyi argued that a rational person behind a veil of ignorance should treat each social position as equally likely and so maximise expected utility, which is equivalent to choosing the principle that maximises average utility. Maximin, which looks only at the worst outcome, is in his view irrationally cautious: it would reject a society where almost everyone does far better merely because the worst-off do slightly worse. Rawls replies that the case is special: the choice fixes one's whole life prospects and basic liberties, there is no basis for probabilities, and parties must be able to honour the agreement. Principles that might sacrifice some for others impose intolerable strains of commitment.

questions.q: What does Charles Mills mean by calling ideal theory 'ideology'?
markScheme: Ideal theory abstracts from actual injustice, idealising agents, institutions and assuming full compliance
Such abstraction leaves out the realities of oppression, e.g. racial domination, so its concepts do not fit the actual social world
Ideology: it reflects and serves the perspective of the privileged who do not experience oppression, while appearing neutral
Mills favours non-ideal theory that starts from actual injustice (e.g. corrective racial justice), while still seeking to reclaim liberalism
questions.modelAnswer: In 'Ideal Theory as Ideology' (2005) Mills argues that mainstream political philosophy works with idealised models: rational, equal individuals; just institutions; full compliance. These models are not neutral simplifications, because they leave out exactly what matters most to oppressed groups, such as racial domination, exclusion and the historical injustices behind current distributions. This is ideological in the Marxist sense: theory that reflects the experience and interests of the privileged comes to look like universal reasoning. Mills does not reject liberalism; he calls for a non-ideal liberalism that starts from actual injustice and asks what corrective justice requires.

questions.q: Explain G.A. Cohen's incentives critique of Rawls's difference principle, including his kidnapper analogy, and assess one reply.
markScheme: Rawls allows inequalities when incentives for the talented raise the position of the worst off
Cohen: the inequality is necessary only because the talented choose to withhold effort unless paid more; it is not necessary independently of their will

Kidnapper analogy: 'pay or the child suffers' may be a valid argument as stated by a third party, but cannot be justified by the kidnapper face to face; likewise the talented cannot justify their demand to the poor
Conclusion: a just society requires an egalitarian ethos in personal choices, not only just institutions
Reply and assessment, e.g. Rawls/Pogge: justice applies only to the basic structure; or the demand would violate freedom of occupation and personal prerogative; with a judgement on its success
questions.modelAnswer: Rawls allows higher pay for the talented when these incentives make the worst off better off. Cohen notes that the inequality is necessary only because the talented choose not to work as hard for less. A kidnapper cannot justify 'pay me or you lose your child' to the parents, since he makes that premise true; likewise the talented cannot justify their demand face to face to the poor. So justice requires an egalitarian ethos, not only just institutions. Rawlsians reply that justice governs only the basic structure. Cohen's answer, that informal structures such as the gendered family already shape distribution, is strong, though his own personal prerogative blurs where legitimate self-interest ends.

questions.q: Why does Hobbes think the sovereign's power must be absolute and undivided, and what liberties do subjects retain?
markScheme: Without a common power covenants are unenforceable: 'covenants, without the sword, are but words'
Any limit on the sovereign would need a judge above it, leading to infinite regress or a return to the state of nature
Divided sovereignty (e.g. between king and parliament) invites civil war, the worst evil
Subjects keep an inalienable right to self-preservation: they may resist being killed, need not harm or accuse themselves
Other liberties lie where the law is silent; obligation lasts only as long as the sovereign can protect them
questions.modelAnswer: Hobbes thinks peace needs a power that overawes everyone, since 'covenants, without the sword, are but words'. A limited sovereign would need a judge to decide whether it had overstepped its limits; that judge would be the real sovereign, or else disputes would return to violence. Divided sovereignty, as between king and parliament, invites civil war. Yet subjects keep the right of self-preservation, which no covenant can give up: they may resist those who come to kill or wound them and need not accuse themselves. Other liberties lie where the law is silent, and obligation ends when the sovereign can no longer protect them.

questions.q: Explain Parfit's levelling down objection and show how a prioritarian and a deontic egalitarian would each respond to it.
markScheme: Levelling down: making the better off worse off without benefiting anyone removes inequality
If inequality is intrinsically bad (telic egalitarianism), levelling down is better in at least one respect, which many find absurd
Prioritarian response: give up equality as such; benefits matter more the worse off a person is in absolute terms, so levelling down is in no way better
Deontic egalitarian response: inequality is objectionable only when produced by unjust agency, so a natural or harmless fall in others' welfare is not an improvement
Some egalitarians (e.g. Temkin) bite the bullet: levelling down is better in one respect though worse all things considered
questions.modelAnswer: Levelling down reduces inequality only by lowering the better off, with no gain to anyone, as when the sighted lose their sight so that they are no better off than the blind. If inequality is bad in itself (telic egalitarianism), this must be better in one respect, which seems absurd since it is better for no one. Prioritarians avoid this by dropping comparison: benefits matter more the worse off someone is, so levelling down is no improvement. Deontic egalitarians object only to inequality produced by unfair agency, so there is no impersonal value in levelling down. Temkin bites the bullet: levelling down is better in one respect though worse overall.

questions.q: A robber says to you, 'Your money or your life', and you hand over your wallet. Did the robber make you unfree? Assess the case on a pure negative account, a moralised account and a republican account of freedom, and say which you find most persuasive.
markScheme: Pure negative (Steiner/Carter): unfreedom requires an action being made impossible; threats do not remove options, they change their costs, so strictly you remained free to refuse
Hobbes concurs that acting from fear is compatible with liberty
Moralised account: the threat is an unjust interference, so it reduces freedom; but this makes judgements of freedom depend on prior judgements of justice (Cohen's criticism)
Republican account: the robber subjects you to arbitrary power; you are unfree because you are dominated, even before he acts
Critical comparison, e.g. pure view gives counter-intuitive verdict; moralised view risks circularity; republican view captures intuition but may overextend unfreedom
A reasoned final judgement
questions.modelAnswer: On a pure negative account (Steiner, Carter), I am unfree to do something only if it is made impossible. The robber made keeping my wallet costly, not impossible, so strictly I stayed free to refuse; Hobbes likewise holds that fear and liberty are consistent. A moralised account counts the unjust threat as reducing freedom, matching intuition, but, as Cohen argued, it makes freedom depend on prior judgements of justice. A republican account says I was unfree because I was subject to the robber's arbitrary will, even before he acted. The pure view helps measure options, but the republican view best explains the wrong of being at another's mercy, without the moralised view's circularity.

questions.q: 'Freedom is simply the absence of interference by other people. Anyone who calls poverty, ignorance or dependence a lack of freedom is confusing liberty with some other value.' Discuss with reference to at least two theorists of liberty.
markScheme: Clear statement of the negative conception (Berlin, Hobbes) and the proposition's link to Berlin's warning against conflating values
Explains Berlin's reasons: value pluralism, honesty about trade-offs, fear of positive liberty's 'true self' justifications for coercion
Positive liberty challenge: Taylor's exercise concept, internal constraints, need to judge the significance of freedoms
Cohen's 'Freedom and Money': poverty itself involves exposure to interference, so even on negative terms it restricts freedom
Republican challenge: dependence on arbitrary power is unfreedom without interference (Pettit, Skinner)
MacCallum: disagreement is about the variables, not about two concepts
Evaluation: weighs clarity and anti-paternalist virtues of the negative view against its counter-intuitive verdicts
Reaches a reasoned conclusion that answers the proposition directly
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition restates Berlin's view in 'Two Concepts of Liberty': liberty is the absence of obstruction by others, and 'liberty is liberty, not equality or fairness or justice'. Berlin had two reasons. Value pluralism means that values conflict, and we should admit when redistribution trades away some liberty rather than redefine liberty to hide the loss. And positive liberty, freedom as self-mastery, invites rulers to coerce people in the name of their 'true' selves, as with Rousseau's claim that people may be 'forced to be free'.

The proposition is nevertheless too strong. First, Cohen shows that poverty is not merely a lack of ability. Money works like a ticket: someone without it who tries to take food or board a train will be stopped by others. Lacking money exposes a person to interference, so poverty restricts freedom even on Berlin's own negative terms. Second, Taylor argues that negative liberty cannot avoid judging which freedoms are significant: we do not regard a country with few traffic lights but no freedom of religion as freer than one with many traffic lights and religious liberty. Once significance matters, the agent's ability actually to direct her life enters the picture. Third, republicans such as Pettit argue that dependence is itself unfreedom: a wife under a legal regime of coverture, or a worker who can be dismissed at will, lives at the mercy of another even if that power is never used. The kind master's slave is unfree.

MacCallum's analysis helps to clarify the dispute. Every freedom is freedom of an agent from some constraint to do something, so the argument is about what counts as a constraint, not about two incompatible concepts.

Berlin's warning remains valuable: calling ignorance 'unfreedom' can license paternalism, and clarity about trade-offs matters. But the proposition is wrong to say that poverty and dependence are simply other values. Poverty restricts negative freedom through the threat of interference, and dependence restricts freedom understood as non-domination. Recognising this is not confusion but a more accurate account of what being free requires.

questions.q: The government of the fictional state of Veridia proposes three measures: (a) a 40% tax on sugary drinks, justified by rising rates of type 2 diabetes among adults; (b) a ban on BASE jumping, even on private land with the owner's consent, after three deaths in a year; and (c) a compulsory 48-hour 'cooling-off' period before anyone can take out a high-interest payday loan. Mira, a libertarian campaigner, says all three are 'unjustified paternalism that treats adults as children'. Evaluate Mira's claim for each measure, drawing on the concept of paternalism, Mill's harm principle and debates about the value of liberty.
markScheme: Defines paternalism (interference against a person's will for their own good) and distinguishes soft from hard paternalism
Mill's harm principle: one's own good is not a sufficient warrant; self-regarding conduct is protected

Measure (a): a tax changes the cost of options rather than prohibiting them; possible non-paternalistic justifications (costs to a public health system, harm to others) and whether these are genuinely 'harm' in Mill's sense
Measure (b): an outright ban on a risky but informed, voluntary activity is hard paternalism; Mill would oppose it; possible counter-arguments (third-party costs to rescuers)
Measure (c): a cooling-off period is plausibly soft paternalism, aiming to ensure decisions are voluntary and informed; compares with Mill's unsafe bridge example
Notes the value of liberty: individuality, experiments of living, autonomy as intrinsic value
Considers counter-arguments: behavioural evidence on weakness of will; positive liberty views supporting intervention; Berlin's warning about 'true self' paternalism
Evaluation that distinguishes the measures rather than treating them as a block, and a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Paternalism is interference with a person's liberty against their will, justified by their own good (Gerald Dworkin). Mill rejects it for competent adults: a person's own good is 'not a sufficient warrant' for coercion, and over himself the individual is sovereign. But Mill also allowed some interference to ensure that choices are genuinely the person's own, the distinction now drawn between soft and hard paternalism. Mira's claim treats three different measures as if they were the same.

Measure (b) is the clearest case of hard paternalism. BASE jumpers know the risks, act voluntarily and, on private land with consent, harm no one else. Mill would condemn the ban: risky self-regarding pursuits are 'experiments of living' through which people develop individuality. The state might cite costs to rescue services, but Mill held that merely 'constructive' injury to society should be borne for the sake of liberty. Mira is right here.

Measure (a) is weaker interference: a tax does not forbid buying drinks but makes it more expensive. If justified by drinkers' own health, it is paternalistic, though it leaves the choice open. A non-paternalistic justification is available: in a publicly funded health system, diet-related illness imposes costs on others. Whether that counts as harm in Mill's sense is debatable, since almost any self-regarding choice has some cost to others, and stretching harm this far would empty the principle. Mira's charge has partial force.

Measure (c) is the best candidate for soft paternalism. Payday borrowing is often done under acute stress, and evidence of present bias suggests many such choices do not reflect the borrower's settled preferences. Like Mill's unsafe bridge, where we may stop someone briefly to make sure they know the danger, a short delay checks that the choice is informed and considered without overriding it. After 48 hours the adult decides.

Berlin would warn that appeals to what people 'really' want can license domination, and that warning applies most to (a) and (b). Overall, Mira is right about the ban, partly right about the tax, and wrong about the cooling-off period, which respects rather than overrides adult agency.

questions.q: 'A worker who can be dismissed at will is unfree, even if her employer is kind and never threatens her.' Critically assess this claim. In your answer, compare negative and republican conceptions of liberty and consider what the claim would imply for the relationship between liberty and economic equality.
markScheme: Sets out the negative conception: unfreedom requires actual (or probable) interference; a kind employer reduces little freedom
Considers sophisticated negative replies: probability of interference, Carter/Kramer's view that dependence reduces overall freedom via likely future prevention
Sets out republican freedom as non-domination (Pettit, Skinner): exposure to arbitrary power is itself unfreedom; benevolent master case
Applies to employment: at-will dismissal gives arbitrary power; self-censorship, deference, strategic ingratiation
