Objections to republicanism: what counts as 'arbitrary'; risk of moralising freedom; whether exit options (a competitive labour market) remove domination
Connects to economic equality: material independence, basic income, workplace rights, Rawls's property-owning democracy, Pettit's eyeball test
Considers libertarian response: employment is a voluntary contract; freedom of contract and exit
Evaluation of which conception better explains the intuitions in the case
Clear structure and a reasoned conclusion that engages with the implications
questions.modelAnswer:
On a negative conception, the kind employer barely affects the worker's freedom. She is unfree only if someone prevents or threatens to prevent her actions, and her employer does neither. A libertarian adds that the contract was voluntary and she can leave. So the claim looks false.

Republicans such as Pettit and Skinner disagree. Freedom is non-domination: not living subject to another's capacity to interfere arbitrarily, that is, at their discretion and unchecked by the interests of the person affected. The slave of a kind master is the classic case. He is unfree not because he is interfered with but because he must keep his master happy. The at-will worker resembles him in an important respect: she may watch what she says, avoid joining a union, flatter her manager and accept unpaid overtime, adjusting her conduct to his will. Domination produces these effects even without threats, which a pure non-interference view cannot register.

Negative theorists have replies. Carter and Kramer argue that dependence lowers a person's overall freedom because it raises the probability of future prevention, so the negative view can register much of what republicans say. But this makes the worker's freedom depend on the employer's temperament, which is precisely the republican's complaint. The more serious objection is about exit: if the labour market is competitive and welfare provision generous, dismissal is not catastrophic and the employer's power is not domination. This is right, but it supports the claim's conditional form. Whether at-will employment dominates depends on the worker's alternatives.

This is where liberty and equality meet. If freedom is non-domination, securing it requires material independence: enough resources, legal protections and alternatives that no one must defer to another to live. Unfair dismissal rights, strong unions, a basic income or Rawls's property-owning democracy, which disperses capital ownership in advance, all reduce domination. Pettit's 'eyeball test' makes the point vividly: citizens should be able to look each other in the eye without fear or deference. On this view economic equality is not a rival to liberty but one of its conditions.

I conclude that the claim is true if read conditionally: the worker is unfree to the extent that dismissal would leave her without acceptable alternatives. The republican conception explains this better than the negative one, and its implication is that a society serious about liberty must also be serious about reducing economic dependence.

questions.q: 'Equality of opportunity is the only kind of equality a just society should pursue; once everyone has a fair start, unequal outcomes are deserved.' Discuss.
markScheme: Distinguishes formal and fair (substantive) equality of opportunity
Explains the appeal of the proposition: respects responsibility, choice and desert; compatible with liberty and markets
Problem of natural talents: Rawls argues talent is morally arbitrary, so even fair equality of opportunity rewards luck
The family problem: fair equality of opportunity is never fully achievable while families transmit advantage, and full achievement would threaten family liberty
Desert critique: Young's meritocracy satire; effort itself shaped by circumstance
Alternative currencies: luck egalitarianism (Dworkin, Cohen), sufficiency, relational equality (Anderson), political equality
Considers whether unequal outcomes undermine future opportunity and political equality
Evaluation and reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition expresses a popular meritocratic view. If everyone has a genuinely fair start, then differences in outcome reflect effort and choice, which people can be held responsible for. It also fits with liberty: once the start is fair, people may use their talents and trade freely.

The first difficulty is what counts as a fair start. Formal equality of opportunity, careers open to talents, removes legal barriers but leaves class advantage intact. Rawls's fair equality of opportunity requires that people with similar talents and motivation have similar prospects regardless of background. But Rawls himself argued that even this is insufficient, because it still lets income track natural talent, which is as morally arbitrary as social class. No one deserves to be born clever any more than to be born rich. This is why Rawls adds the difference principle, which allows inequalities only when they benefit the least advantaged.

Second, the ideal is unstable. Families pass on advantages through upbringing, networks and inheritance. Achieving full equality of opportunity would require intrusive limits on what parents can do for their children. And unequal outcomes in one generation become unequal opportunities in the next.

Third, the link to desert is weak. Willingness to work hard is itself shaped by upbringing. Michael Young coined 'meritocracy' as a warning: a society convinced that its winners deserve their position may treat losers with contempt.

Other kinds of equality are worth wanting too. Political equality, one person one vote with the fair value of political liberty, is not about opportunity at all. Frankfurt's sufficiency view insists that everyone should have enough, whatever their choices, and Anderson argues that equality concerns relationships free of domination, not just fair races.

Equality of opportunity is an essential part of justice, but it cannot be the whole of it. Because talents are unearned and starting points can never be fully equalised, unequal outcomes are not automatically deserved. A just society also needs limits on inequality of outcome, a social minimum and protections for political equality.

questions.q: A society can adopt one of three economic schemes. Its population divides into three equally sized groups, and the figures below give each group's index of wellbeing (higher is better). Scheme A: 20, 20, 20. Scheme B: 25, 40, 70. Scheme C: 18, 60, 120. (i) Identify which scheme would be preferred by strict telic egalitarianism, Rawls's difference principle, classical (total) utilitarianism, and sufficientarianism with a threshold of 20, showing your working. (ii) Explain what the move from B to A illustrates about egalitarianism. (iii) Evaluate which principle gives the most defensible verdict.
markScheme: Strict telic egalitarianism: A, the only equal distribution
Difference principle: B, since its worst-off group (25) is better off than in A (20) or C (18)
Total utilitarianism: C, totals A=60, B=135, C=198
Sufficientarianism (threshold 20): A and B both bring everyone to the threshold; C does not (18), so C is ruled out and the view is indifferent between A and B above the threshold
Prioritarianism noted: verdict depends on the weighting; strong priority favours B, weak priority may favour C
Move from B to A makes every group worse off (25 to 20, 40 to 20, 70 to 20): a case of levelling down (Parfit); telic egalitarian must say A is better in one respect

Evaluation of the difference principle (efficiency plus concern for the worst off) against utilitarianism (separateness of persons, sacrifice of the worst off in C) and egalitarianism (levelling down)
Considers objections to the difference principle, e.g. it ignores large gains to others if the worst off gain slightly; Harsanyi
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
(i) Strict telic egalitarianism prefers A, the only distribution with no inequality. Rawls's difference principle ranks schemes by the position of the least advantaged: the worst-off group gets 20 in A, 25 in B and 18 in C, so B is chosen. Total utilitarianism adds up wellbeing: A = 60, B = 25 + 40 + 70 = 135, C = 18 + 60 + 120 = 198, so C wins. A sufficientarian with a threshold of 20 rules out C, where one group falls to 18, but is indifferent between A and B, since everyone has enough in both. A prioritarian's verdict depends on the weight given to the worse off: with strong priority B wins, and with mild priority the large gains in C may outweigh the loss of 7 points to the worst off.

(ii) Moving from B to A makes every group worse off: 25 falls to 20, 40 to 20 and 70 to 20. The only 'gain' is the removal of inequality. This is Parfit's levelling down objection. If inequality is bad in itself, A must be better than B in at least one respect, yet it is better for no one. Most people find that implausible, which suggests that what we care about is not equality as such but the condition of the worse off, or the avoidance of unfair relations.

(iii) Utilitarianism's choice of C shows Rawls's separateness of persons objection: the worst-off group is made worse off than under any alternative in order to produce gains for others, as if society were one person balancing losses against gains. Strict egalitarianism's choice of A is vulnerable to levelling down. Sufficiency gives too little guidance, since it cannot choose between A and B, though B is better for everyone. The difference principle's choice of B combines efficiency with concern for the worst off: it accepts inequality only when it benefits those at the bottom.

The difference principle is not beyond criticism. It would prefer a scheme giving the worst off 26 and everyone else 27 to one giving them 25 and others 1,000, which many find too extreme, and Harsanyi argues that rational choosers would maximise average utility. Yet in this choice the difference principle gives the most defensible verdict. B is better for every group than A and does not sacrifice the worst off, as C does.

questions.q: 'The point of equality is not to compensate people for bad luck, but to end oppression and allow people to stand in relations of equality with one another.' Critically evaluate this claim, comparing luck egalitarian and relational accounts of equality.
markScheme: Explains luck egalitarianism: neutralise brute luck, hold people responsible for option luck (Dworkin, Arneson, Cohen); 'currency' debate (resources, welfare, access to advantage)
Explains Anderson's relational/democratic equality: equality as a social relationship; capabilities for functioning as an equal citizen; opposing oppression, domination and status hierarchy

Anderson's objections: abandonment of negligent victims; discrimination against the disabled and naturally unlucky (pity, the 'letter from the State Equality Board'); intrusive judgements of responsibility
Luck egalitarian replies: can be supplemented by sufficiency/humanitarian concerns; responsibility tracks fairness; Cohen: luck egalitarianism describes justice, not all values a state must honour
Problems for relational equality: indeterminacy about distribution; tolerates large material inequality above a threshold; may still need responsibility judgements
Links to other theorists: Young's critique of the distributive paradigm; Scheffler; Fraser on recognition
Considers hybrid positions
Sustained evaluation and a defended conclusion
Clear structure with accurate use of authorities
questions.modelAnswer:
Luck egalitarians such as Dworkin, Arneson and Cohen hold that inequalities are unjust when they reflect brute luck, unchosen circumstances like disability or class of birth, but may be fair when they reflect choices for which people are responsible. The theory captures a powerful intuition: it is unfair for some to be worse off through no fault of their own.

Elizabeth Anderson's 'What Is the Point of Equality?' attacks this view. First, it is too harsh: a reckless, uninsured driver who causes a crash seems to have no claim to emergency treatment, since his plight results from option luck. Second, it is demeaning: compensating people for being born untalented or disabled requires the state to certify them as inferior, which Anderson dramatises as a letter from an imagined State Equality Board. Third, it requires intrusive judgements about who is responsible for what. She proposes democratic equality instead. The aim is to abolish oppressive hierarchies of domination, exploitation and status, and to guarantee everyone the capabilities needed to function as an equal citizen.

Luck egalitarians have replies. Most combine luck egalitarianism with a humanitarian floor, so the reckless driver is treated. Cohen argued that luck egalitarianism tells us what justice is, not everything the state should do, so other values can override it. And relational equality cannot avoid distribution: whether wealth inequalities undermine equal standing depends on how large they are, and Anderson's threshold view seems to tolerate large inequalities above it. Relational theorists also need some idea of responsibility, for example when deciding whether unemployment benefits should depend on seeking work.

Anderson's challenge nonetheless exposes something luck egalitarianism misses. Many of the gravest injustices, such as racial segregation, coverture, caste and workplace domination, are wrongs in relationships rather than unlucky distributions. Iris Marion Young similarly criticised the 'distributive paradigm' for overlooking oppression, and Fraser shows that status injustice cannot be reduced to maldistribution. A theory centred on brute luck struggles to say why a well-compensated subordinate group is still treated unjustly.

I conclude that the claim is largely right about the point of equality but overstated. Ending oppression and securing equal standing is the more basic aim, which explains why equality matters politically. But luck matters too: within a society of equals it remains unfair for some to bear heavy unchosen disadvantages. The best view is relational at its foundation and sensitive to luck in its distributive principles.

questions.q: 'Taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor' (Nozick). Assess this claim and what it implies about whether liberty and equality can be reconciled.
markScheme: Explains Nozick's argument: taking n hours of earnings is like forcing n hours of work for others; it gives others partial property rights in the person, violating self-ownership
Places it within the entitlement theory and the claim that 'liberty upsets patterns'
Disanalogies: the taxed person chooses whether and how much to work and in what job; forced labour removes that choice
Nozick's own anticipation: the taxed person has options, but so does someone forced to work n hours, for whose purpose is decisive
Objection: earnings depend on a legal and social framework (property, contract, markets) that taxation partly defines; Murphy and Nagel's 'myth of ownership'
Cohen: libertarianism relies on a moralised view of freedom; property itself restricts the freedom of non-owners
Rawlsian response: just background institutions set entitlements in advance; occupational freedom preserved
Implication for reconciliation: if Nozick is right, liberty and equality conflict deeply; if earnings are defined by just institutions, much of the conflict dissolves
Evaluation and conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Nozick's claim follows from self-ownership. If I own myself, I own my labour and what I freely receive in exchange for it. Taxing the earnings of n hours of work for redistribution is like forcing me to work n hours for others, and it makes others part-owners of me. Combined with the entitlement theory and the claim that 'liberty upsets patterns', the argument implies that liberty and equality are fundamentally opposed: any patterned distribution must be maintained by continual violation of people's rights.

The analogy has force. A tax on earnings does mean that part of my working life goes to purposes I did not choose. But there are significant disanalogies. The forced labourer cannot choose whether to work, what work to do or when to stop. The taxpayer chooses all of these and simply keeps less of the reward. Nozick anticipates this reply, observing that someone forced to work could be given a choice of tasks and would still be coerced. Yet the degree of control over one's life clearly differs, and this matters if self-ownership is valued because it protects autonomy.

A deeper objection is that the argument assumes pre-tax earnings are already fully mine. Murphy and Nagel call this the 'myth of ownership': pre-tax income is produced under a legal framework of property, contract, money and enforcement that the state creates, and the tax system is part of that framework. Rawls's position is similar: entitlements are what people are due under just background institutions, so they are not seized after the fact.

Cohen adds that Nozick's case relies on a moralised conception of freedom. Private property itself restricts the freedom of non-owners, who are excluded from what others own. Enforcing property is therefore not neutral between liberty and coercion; it distributes freedom.

These replies suggest reconciliation is possible. If entitlements are defined by just institutions and freedom of occupation is protected, taxation for fair equality of opportunity or the difference principle is not like forced labour. Nozick is right that redistribution has a cost to individual control over one's life. But he is wrong to treat that cost as absolute, and wrong to assume that the market distribution embodies liberty. Liberty and equality conflict at the margin, not at the root.

questions.q: 'Liberty and equality are not rivals: properly understood, each requires the other.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out the conflict thesis: Nozick (liberty upsets patterns), Hayek (material equality requires unequal treatment), Berlin (values conflict)
Rawls: lexical priority of liberty, distinction between liberty and its worth, fair value of political liberty, property-owning democracy
Cohen: money and freedom; property restricts the freedom of non-owners
Republican argument: non-domination requires material independence
Dworkin: equality as sovereign virtue; liberty and equality cannot conflict when properly defined
Critique of 'properly understood': risk of redefining terms to dissolve conflict (Berlin's warning, Hart on Rawls)
Considers the argument from the other side: equality requiring liberty (equal basic liberties, political equality, Wollstonecraft and Mill on women)
Evaluation distinguishing which liberties and which kinds of equality conflict
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The conflict thesis has prominent defenders. Nozick argues that free exchanges disrupt any egalitarian pattern, so equality must be enforced against liberty. Hayek holds that people differ, so making them materially equal requires treating them unequally under the law. Berlin, more moderately, insists that liberty and equality are distinct values that sometimes clash, and that honesty requires admitting losses.

The proposition has strong support, however. First, equality requires liberty. Equal citizenship is constituted by equal basic liberties: conscience, expression, the vote. Wollstonecraft and Mill argued that women's subordination was both a denial of liberty and of equality, and could only be remedied by securing both. Rawls's first principle is itself an equality principle, equal basic liberties for all.

Second, liberty arguably requires equality. Cohen shows that money is a ticket against interference, so redistribution redistributes freedom. Rawls distinguishes liberty from its worth and insists that the political liberties have fair value, which limits the influence of wealth on politics. Republicans argue that freedom as non-domination requires material independence: a person who depends on another's goodwill to survive is not free. Rawls's property-owning democracy aims to disperse capital so that all can be independent.

Yet the phrase 'properly understood' needs scrutiny. Dworkin argues that once liberty is understood as a right to freedoms consistent with equal concern, it cannot conflict with equality. Berlin would say this wins the argument by definition: some genuine liberties, such as the freedom to bequeath wealth or to buy private education, really are restricted by egalitarian policy. Hart pressed a similar point against Rawls, arguing that the priority of liberty does not resolve conflicts that arise among liberties themselves.

The best conclusion is a qualified one. Basic liberties and political equality are mutually supporting: each is incomplete without the other. Economic equality and the liberty of non-owners also support each other. But some economic liberties, especially over the use and transfer of property, do conflict with material equality. So the two values are not rivals at their core, but they compete at the edges, and political philosophy must judge those trade-offs rather than define them away.

questions.q: The fictional government of Aldria proposes three reforms: (1) a 65% top rate of income tax above £200,000 a year to fund a universal basic income of £9,000 per adult; (2) a cap of £5,000 per person per year on donations to political parties and campaigns; (3) the abolition of fee-paying schools. Opposition MP Tom Hargreaves says: 'Each reform sacrifices liberty to equality.' Minister Leila Osei replies: 'Each reform protects someone's liberty.' Assess who has the better of the argument for each reform, drawing on at least three of: Nozick, Rawls, Berlin, Cohen and republican theory.
markScheme: Frames the debate: conflict thesis vs reconciliation; whose liberty is at stake in each case
Reform 1, Hargreaves: Nozick's taxation-as-forced-labour and self-ownership; Berlin on honest trade-offs
Reform 1, Osei: Cohen (money as freedom); republican material independence (exit option from dominating work); Rawls's worth of liberty
Reform 2, Hargreaves: restriction on political expression and association
Reform 2, Osei: Rawls's fair value of political liberties; political equality; prevents wealth from buying influence
Reform 3, Hargreaves: restricts parental liberty and freedom of association; possible clash with family autonomy
Reform 3, Osei: fair equality of opportunity; children's future liberty; but considers whether abolition is necessary or whether less restrictive means exist; family's legitimate role
Distinguishes basic liberties (expression, association) from economic liberties, noting Rawls's view that the latter have weaker protection
Weighs the strength of each side reform by reform, rather than one blanket answer
Overall conclusion with clear reasoning
questions.modelAnswer:
Hargreaves expresses the conflict thesis; Osei claims that each reform redistributes liberty rather than sacrificing it. The answer differs across the reforms.

(1) Tax and basic income. For Nozick, taxing high earnings to fund transfers is on a par with forced labour, and it violates self-ownership. Berlin would accept that redistribution can be justified but insist that the top earners lose some liberty. Osei has strong replies. Cohen argues that money is a ticket against interference: the £9,000 grant expands the negative freedom of recipients more than the tax restricts high earners, who remain wealthy. Republicans add that a basic income gives workers an exit option from dominating employers or partners. Rawls would describe the reform as raising the worth of liberty for the least advantaged. Osei wins on balance: liberty is redistributed, though Hargreaves is right that high earners lose some.

(2) Donation cap. This looks like a restriction on expression and association, both basic liberties in Rawls's first principle, so Hargreaves's objection is more serious here. But Rawls also holds that the political liberties must have fair value: citizens similarly motivated must have roughly equal chances to influence policy. Unlimited donations let wealth buy political power, undermining political equality. Rawls himself suggested public funding and contribution limits. The cap protects the political liberty of poorer citizens. Osei wins.

(3) Abolishing fee-paying schools. This is the hardest case. It restricts parents' freedom to spend money on their children and schools' freedom of association. In its favour, fair equality of opportunity is badly undermined when wealth buys educational advantage, and children's future liberties depend on their education. But Rawls ranks fair equality of opportunity below basic liberties, and some parental partiality is part of valuable family life. The key question is whether abolition is necessary, or whether lesser measures, such as removing tax advantages and improving state schools, would serve opportunity at lower cost to liberty. Here Hargreaves has the better of the argument: the reform involves a real loss of liberty and equality might be advanced by less restrictive means.

In conclusion, Osei is right that 'liberty versus equality' is often liberty versus liberty, but her claim does not hold equally in all three cases. Reforms (1) and (2) protect the freedom of the many at modest cost; reform (3) sacrifices genuine liberty for equality and needs a stronger justification.

questions.q: 'Hobbes saw clearly what Locke underestimated: without an absolute sovereign, life returns to war.' Compare Hobbes's and Locke's accounts of the state of nature and assess what each implies about the limits of government.
markScheme: Hobbes: equality of vulnerability, scarcity, competition, diffidence and glory; war of all against all; no property or justice without a sovereign
Hobbes's conclusion: rational individuals authorise an absolute, undivided sovereign; only the right to self-preservation is retained
Locke: state of nature governed by natural law known by reason; natural rights to life, liberty and estate; property before government
Locke's 'inconveniences': lack of settled law, impartial judge and enforcement power; state of nature can degenerate into a state of war
Locke's conclusion: limited government held on trust, majority rule, separation of legislative and executive, right of resistance
Assessment of the proposition: Hobbes's insight into insecurity and the need for a final judge; Locke's reply that absolute power exposes subjects to a worse danger (polecats and lions)
Evaluation of which account is more plausible and why, with a conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
For Hobbes, people in the state of nature are roughly equal in their ability to kill each other and compete for scarce goods. Competition, distrust and the desire for glory make pre-emptive attack rational, so the condition is a war of every man against every man in which there is no industry, no property and no justice. The only escape is for each to authorise a sovereign whose power is absolute and undivided, since any limit would need a higher judge and divided power invites civil war. Subjects keep only the right to defend their lives.

Locke's state of nature is governed by a law of nature, known by reason, which forbids harming others in their life, health, liberty or possessions. People already have property through their labour. The problem is not constant war but 'inconveniences': there is no settled law, no impartial judge and no reliable power of enforcement, so people judge their own cases and disputes can escalate into a state of war. Government is created by consent to remedy these defects and holds power on trust. It must govern by standing laws, cannot take property without consent, and may be resisted if it betrays its trust.

The proposition captures a real strength of Hobbes. Without a final authority, disagreements about rights can turn violent, and Locke relies on a natural law that people interpret differently. But Locke has a powerful reply: it is absurd to protect ourselves from polecats or foxes by submitting to a lion. An unchecked sovereign is itself a major source of danger, and Hobbes's subjects have no remedy short of an attack on their lives.

History offers some support to both: civil wars show the cost of collapsing authority, while abuses by absolute rulers show the danger of unchecked power. On balance Locke's account is more persuasive about the limits of government: security requires a common authority, but not an absolute one, and constitutional limits, consent and a right of resistance make government safer rather than weaker.

questions.q: Apply Mill's harm principle to the following cases in the fictional town of Easton. (a) Priya runs a blog arguing, against the medical evidence, that vaccines cause autism; local vaccination rates fall. (b) Dan stands outside the home of a property developer, Mr Clarke, and addresses an angry crowd, shouting that Clarke 'is the reason your children are homeless'. (c) Sam, an adult, takes up an extreme fasting regime that doctors warn may damage his health; he has no dependants. (d) A supermarket refuses to employ anyone who publicly criticises its owners. For each, explain what Mill would say and evaluate whether the harm principle gives a satisfactory answer.
markScheme: States the harm principle and the self-regarding/other-regarding distinction; harm understood as damage to others' interests, not mere offence

(a) Mill's defence of free expression: the truth may emerge, dead dogma; distinguishes publication from incitement; but lowered vaccination may harm others (third-party risk), raising whether indirect harm via others' free choices counts
(b) Close analogy to Mill's corn-dealer example: opinion permissible in print but punishable when delivered to an excited mob outside the house, because it is a positive instigation to harm
(c) Self-regarding conduct: Mill opposes coercion, permits advice, persuasion and warning; possible soft paternalism if Sam is not fully informed (bridge example)
(d) Social sanction and private power: Mill's concern with social tyranny and conformity; employer pressure on opinion; whether law should restrict it
Evaluates difficulties: vagueness of 'harm', the problem of indirect and aggregated harms, whether offence counts
Recognises Mill's utilitarian grounding ('utility in the largest sense')
Clear, case-by-case structure and an overall judgement on the principle's adequacy
questions.modelAnswer:
Mill's harm principle holds that the only legitimate ground for coercing a competent adult is to prevent harm to others; his own good is not a sufficient warrant. Harm means damage to others' interests, not mere offence or disapproval.

(a) Priya. Mill's arguments for free expression apply strongly. Even false opinions should be heard: suppressing them assumes infallibility, and challenge keeps true beliefs alive rather than 'dead dogma'. Mill would allow doctors and others to argue against her as forcefully as they wish. The difficulty is that lower vaccination rates harm third parties, including those who cannot be vaccinated. Mill's framework struggles here, because the harm results from others' free choices to believe her. His likely answer is that the remedy is more speech, not censorship. This seems right for the blog, though a case for restriction becomes stronger if she knowingly makes false claims of fact in commercial advertising.

(b) Dan. This is close to Mill's own example: the opinion that corn dealers starve the poor may be published in the press, but may justly be punished when delivered to an excited mob before a corn dealer's house. The context makes the speech a positive instigation to imminent harm. Mill would permit Dan to write his views but allow intervention here.

(c) Sam. His fasting is self-regarding. Mill would allow others to warn, advise and even avoid him, but not to coerce him. If Sam does not understand the risk, a temporary intervention to inform him, like stopping someone on an unsafe bridge, is permissible. Once he understands, his choice must be respected. This verdict is attractive, though some worry about whether extreme fasting reflects a fully free choice.

(d) The supermarket. Mill feared social tyranny, the pressure of opinion and custom, more than law. Using economic power to punish opinion chills expression in exactly the way he deplored. Whether law should prohibit it is less clear, since it limits the employer's liberty; Mill's concern with conformity suggests some legal protection is defensible.

The harm principle gives clear and plausible answers to (b) and (c). It struggles with (a) and (d), where harms are indirect, aggregated or arise from private power. This shows that the principle needs a fuller account of harm, which Mill grounded in utility 'in the largest sense', rather than a simple test.

questions.q: 'Wollstonecraft's case for women's equality simply applies liberal principles more consistently; it does not challenge them.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out Wollstonecraft's main argument: women are rational, virtue is the same for both sexes, apparent inferiority results from education and dependence
Liberal reading: universal reason and rights, extending Locke and Enlightenment ideals; reply to Rousseau's Emile and to Talleyrand's report on education
Her positive proposals: co-educational national day schools, women's economic independence and professions, citizenship
Challenge reading: critique of the private sphere and marriage as sites of power; dependence corrupts both sexes; anticipates 'personal is political'
Republican reading (non-domination): her concern is with arbitrary power of husbands, rank and wealth, not only rights
Comparison with Mill's The Subjection of Women
Limits: focus on middle-class women; acceptance of motherhood as primary duty for many women; later critiques via class and race
Evaluation and conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), Wollstonecraft argues that women possess reason and that virtue, grounded in reason, is the same for both sexes. Women's apparent inferiority, their vanity and preoccupation with pleasing men, is the product of an education designed to make them attractive dependants. She replies directly to Rousseau, whose Emile proposed that Sophie be educated to please Emile. Her remedy includes co-educational national schooling, opportunities for women to support themselves in professions such as medicine and business, and recognition of women as citizens.

The proposition has much to support it. Wollstonecraft argues from universal premises shared with Locke and the Enlightenment: reason is the mark of humanity, rights belong to rational beings, and arbitrary power is illegitimate. Her complaint is that men who championed the rights of man in the 1790s failed to apply their own principles to women. Read this way, she is a consistent liberal.

Yet her argument goes further than extending rights. She locates subordination in the family and in marriage, which liberals of her time treated as private and natural. She argues that dependence on men's favour corrupts both sexes, producing tyrants and flatterers, and that genuine virtue is impossible without independence. Republican interpreters read her as concerned with domination, being subject to the arbitrary will of a husband, much as she criticised hereditary rank and the corrupting effects of wealth. This anticipates the later feminist insistence that the personal is political, challenging the liberal divide between public and private. Mill's The Subjection of Women (1869) develops a similar critique, arguing that women's 'nature' cannot be known while it is shaped by subordination.

Her challenge has limits. She writes mainly about middle-class women, says little about working-class or enslaved women, and treats motherhood as a central civic duty for many women. Later critiques based on class and race would press beyond her.

On balance, the proposition is half right. Wollstonecraft's premises are liberal, but by applying them to marriage, the family and the formation of character she exposes assumptions that liberalism had left unexamined. Applying liberal principles consistently turned out to require challenging some of liberalism's own boundaries.

questions.q: 'Utilitarianism cannot provide a secure foundation for individual liberty.' Critically assess this claim with reference to Bentham and Mill.
markScheme: Bentham: principle of utility, felicific calculus; rights as legal creations ('nonsense upon stilts'); liberty valued only instrumentally
Shows the worry: if restricting someone's liberty would increase total happiness, utilitarianism seems to require it (e.g. Panopticon, sacrifices of minorities); Rawls's separateness of persons
Mill's attempt: On Liberty grounded in 'utility in the largest sense', the permanent interests of man as a progressive being
Mill's arguments: fallibility and truth, individuality and experiments of living, people are the best judges of their own interests, dangers of social tyranny
Indirect or rule-based reading: general protection of liberty produces more utility than case-by-case calculation; Mill's 'secondary principles'
Tension: is the harm principle absolute or contingent? Mill's exclusions (children, 'barbarians') show the contingency; slavery contract
Higher pleasures and individuality may smuggle in non-utilitarian, perfectionist values
Comparison with rights-based alternatives (Nozick's side constraints, Rawls's priority of liberty) and their own foundations
Evaluation: 'secure' in what sense; contingent but robust vs absolute
Reasoned conclusion with clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
Bentham's utilitarianism judges every action and law by its tendency to increase happiness. He dismissed natural rights as 'nonsense upon stilts': rights are created by law and justified only by their utility. Liberty therefore has no independent standing. If restricting someone's liberty would produce more happiness overall, Bentham's theory appears to require it. Rawls's objection generalises the worry: utilitarianism treats society as a single person, so losses to some, including losses of liberty, can be offset by gains to others.

Mill tried to show that utilitarianism supports a strong principle of liberty. On Liberty rests not on abstract rights but on utility 'in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being'. His arguments are instrumental but powerful. Silencing opinion risks suppressing truth and turns true beliefs into dead dogma. Individuals are usually the best judges of their own interests. Above all, individuality and 'experiments of living' are essential to human development and social progress. On an indirect reading, a society that firmly protects liberty as a rule produces more happiness than one that calculates case by case, since officials make mistakes and majorities are intolerant.

This shows that utilitarianism can provide a robust foundation, but is it secure? Three problems remain. First, the protection is contingent: if circumstances changed so that restricting liberty reliably increased happiness, utilitarian reasoning would endorse it. Mill's own exclusions confirm this. The harm principle applies only to people 'in the maturity of their faculties', and he defended despotism over 'barbarians' if aimed at their improvement. Second, his treatment of the slavery contract, where liberty may be overridden to protect liberty, suggests he values freedom for more than its happiness. Third, his stress on higher pleasures and individuality looks like a perfectionist ideal of human development, not a neutral sum of pleasures, so his foundation may not be purely utilitarian at all.

Rights-based alternatives face their own difficulties. Nozick's side constraints rest on self-ownership, which he does not fully defend, and Rawls's priority of liberty was challenged by Hart. A contingent foundation may be no worse than an unexplained one.

The claim is therefore largely correct if 'secure' means unconditional. Utilitarianism can justify a strong, durable presumption in favour of liberty, but it cannot make liberty immune from trade-offs. Mill's most persuasive arguments draw on values, autonomy and individual development, that go beyond Bentham's utilitarianism.

questions.q: Set out Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument and evaluate whether it refutes patterned theories of distributive justice.
markScheme: Accurate reconstruction: start with a just distribution D1 (any pattern); a million fans each pay 25 cents to watch Chamberlain; he gains $250,000; resulting D2
Argument: D1 just + voluntary transfers, no third party's share taken; so D2 just; 'liberty upsets patterns'
Conclusion: patterned principles require continual interference with free choices; supports historical entitlement theory
Objection: third-party effects and the cumulative power of wealth (Cohen); fans did not consent to the resulting distribution's effects
Objection: D1 shares need not include full rights of transfer; justice in transfer presupposes a property regime (Nagel, Murphy and Nagel)
Rawlsian reply: background justice of the basic structure; tax rules known in advance, so no transaction-by-transaction interference
Evaluation: shows patterns have costs, but not that they are unjust; begs the question about the content of property rights
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Nozick asks us to imagine any distribution D1 that the reader thinks just, perhaps an equal one. Wilt Chamberlain, a star basketball player, signs a contract under which 25 cents of each ticket goes to him. A million fans pay happily, and Chamberlain ends up with $250,000, far more than anyone else. Call the new distribution D2. If D1 was just, and each person freely chose to transfer part of their just share, how can D2 be unjust? No one else's share was taken. Nozick concludes that 'liberty upsets patterns': any patterned principle can be maintained only by continually interfering with people's choices or forbidding 'capitalist acts between consenting adults'. Justice is historical: what matters is how holdings arose.

The argument is powerful because it uses the egalitarian's own starting point. But there are several replies. First, Cohen argues that the fans consented to give 25 cents, not to the effects of the resulting distribution. Chamberlain's wealth may give him power over others, including future generations who never agreed to anything. Third parties are affected after all. Second, the argument assumes that a just share in D1 includes the full right to transfer it without tax. A patterned theorist can say that justice gives people only qualified property rights, so the fans' payments were always subject to tax. Nozick must presuppose the very conception of ownership in dispute. Third, Rawls replies that justice regulates the basic structure. If tax rules are public and stable, people make their exchanges knowing what they will keep, and there is no constant interference with particular transactions. Rawls also argued that individually fair transactions can, over time, undermine background justice, which is why institutions must correct for their cumulative effects.

The argument does show something important: maintaining a pattern imposes some limits on liberty, and egalitarians must justify them. But it does not refute patterned theories, because its conclusion depends on an absolute conception of property that it assumes rather than defends. It shows a cost of patterns, not their injustice.

questions.q: Imagine you are a party in Rawls's original position, choosing between three schemes for organising society. Each has three equally sized social positions, with lifetime prospects (in units of primary goods) as follows. Scheme X: 30, 40, 50. Scheme Y: 20, 60, 100. Scheme Z: 5, 80, 200. You do not know which position you will occupy, and you have no basis for estimating probabilities. (i) Show which scheme maximin selects and which scheme maximising expected (average) value selects, assuming equal probability for each position. (ii) Explain Rawls's arguments for why maximin is rational in this situation. (iii) Evaluate Harsanyi's objection and decide which reasoning is more persuasive.
markScheme: Maximin: compare worst outcomes, X=30, Y=20, Z=5, so selects X
Expected value with equal probability: X=(30+40+50)/3=40; Y=(20+60+100)/3=60; Z=(5+80+200)/3=95; selects Z
Explains the veil of ignorance and why parties choose principles rather than schemes, including knowledge of general facts
Rawls's three conditions: no reliable probabilities; little concern for gains above a satisfactory minimum; alternatives risk unacceptable outcomes
Further Rawlsian arguments: strains of commitment, publicity and stability, the social bases of self-respect
Harsanyi: principle of insufficient reason, equal probabilities, maximise average utility; maximin is irrationally risk-averse
Critique of Rawls: maximin could reject large gains for many for tiny gains for the worst off; parties don't know their risk attitudes
Critique of Harsanyi: assigning equal probabilities when there is no basis is itself questionable; Z's worst position may be intolerable; separateness of persons
Notes that the difference principle need not rely solely on maximin (Rawls's later emphasis on reciprocity and stability)
Reasoned conclusion on which choice is defensible
questions.modelAnswer:
(i) Maximin ranks schemes by their worst outcomes: X guarantees at least 30, Y 20 and Z only 5. Maximin selects X. If instead each position is assigned a one-third probability, expected values are X = (30 + 40 + 50)/3 = 40, Y = (20 + 60 + 100)/3 = 60, and Z = (5 + 80 + 200)/3 = 95. An expected-value maximiser selects Z.

(ii) Rawls argues that maximin is rational in the original position because of three special conditions. First, the veil removes any basis for estimating probabilities, and Rawls denies that the parties should simply assume equal likelihoods. Second, the parties care relatively little about what they might gain above a satisfactory minimum, since the first principle and the guaranteed social minimum secure what really matters. Third, the alternatives risk outcomes that one could hardly accept: in Z, someone must live with 5 units. Rawls adds the strains of commitment: parties must choose principles they could honour whatever their position, and someone in Z's bottom position could not reasonably be asked to accept it for the sake of others' gains. Public principles that guarantee everyone a decent position also foster stability and self-respect.

(iii) Harsanyi argues that, in the absence of information, rational choice assigns equal probabilities and maximises expected utility, so the parties would choose average utilitarianism and Z. Maximin is excessively risk-averse: it would reject a scheme that gives most people enormous gains whenever the worst off lose slightly. This objection exposes a real weakness, since Rawls's parties are not supposed to know their attitudes to risk, so maximin's appeal cannot be temperamental caution.

Yet Harsanyi's reasoning has problems too. The principle of insufficient reason produces precise probabilities out of ignorance, which is questionable when one's entire life is at stake and the choice is irreversible. More fundamentally, choosing Z treats the person in the bottom position as someone whose loss can be offset by others' gains, which ignores the separateness of persons. Rawls later placed less weight on maximin and more on reciprocity and stability.

I find X the more defensible choice in this case. The decision is a one-off and binding for life, and the worst outcome under Z is severe. However, maximin is not a general rule of rationality; its strength lies in the special features of choosing principles for a whole society.

questions.q: 'If the difference principle is a principle of justice, it must govern not only institutions but also the choices people make within them.' Critically evaluate this claim, drawing on Rawls and G.A. Cohen.
markScheme: Rawls: the basic structure as the primary subject of justice; difference principle permits incentive inequalities that benefit the worst off
Cohen's incentives argument: inequality 'necessary' only given the talented's choices; the kidnapper analogy and the interpersonal test
Cohen's argument that the basic structure cannot be limited to coercive institutions: the family and informal norms shape distribution (the feminist point 'the personal is political')
Cohen's conclusion: a just society requires an egalitarian ethos
Rawlsian replies: division of moral labour; publicity and determinacy of institutional rules; respect for personal freedom and occupational choice
Personal prerogative: Cohen allows some self-interest, raising the question of where the line falls
Pareto argument and the trilemma of equality, Pareto optimality and freedom of occupation
Assesses whether an ethos can be required as a matter of justice versus virtue
Evaluation and a defended conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Rawls holds that the primary subject of justice is the basic structure, the major institutions that distribute rights, duties and the benefits of cooperation. The difference principle therefore allows inequalities that serve as incentives, provided they make the worst off better off than they would otherwise be.

Cohen argues that this is inconsistent. Incentive inequalities are necessary only because talented people choose to work less productively unless paid more. If they genuinely accepted the difference principle, they would not demand more than equal shares, since that would not be necessary for the worst off. His kidnapper analogy shows the problem: an argument whose key premise is made true by the speaker's own choice cannot be offered justifiably to those it disadvantages. In a society whose members share a principle of justice, the talented cannot look the poor in the eye and say 'I will work harder only if paid more, so inequality benefits you.'

Cohen also challenges the boundary of the basic structure. If it includes only coercive legal institutions, it excludes the family, yet the gendered division of labour within families has major distributive effects. If it includes informal structures like the family, then it already reaches choices and norms. Either way, justice cannot be confined to the legal framework. He concludes that a just society requires an egalitarian ethos guiding people's economic choices.

Rawlsians reply in several ways. A division of moral labour lets institutions secure justice while people pursue their own projects, which is crucial for personal freedom. Institutional rules are public and determinate in a way that an ethos is not, which matters for fairness and stability. And requiring people to choose the socially most productive job threatens freedom of occupation. Cohen concedes a personal prerogative to pursue self-interest to some reasonable degree, but this concession is significant: once allowed, the line between legitimate prerogative and unjust incentive-seeking is unclear.

I conclude that the claim is largely correct. A person who sincerely endorses the difference principle cannot consistently bargain for inequality that is not truly necessary, so the principle has implications for personal choice. But these implications are best understood as limits on individuals' reasons, protected by a personal prerogative, rather than as duties that institutions could enforce. Justice has a personal dimension, but not one that erases the importance of institutions.

questions.q: On an uninhabited island, a group of settlers arrives. Mara, the first ashore, fences off and starts to irrigate land around the only freshwater spring, producing far more food than she needs. She offers the others water in exchange for their labour on her farm, at a rate that leaves them better off than they would be if the spring had remained unowned and everyone had scrambled for it. Mara insists she has a just entitlement. Assess her claim using Locke's theory of property, Nozick's entitlement theory and its version of the Lockean proviso, and at least one critic.
markScheme: Locke: self-ownership and labour mixing; Mara has mixed labour with the land; but the sufficiency proviso is breached since there is no 'enough, and as good' water left; spoilage proviso relevant to surplus
Locke's caveat about necessity: elsewhere he holds that the needy have a claim to others' surplus (charity), and a water monopoly would be problematic
Nozick: justice in acquisition, transfer and rectification; his weaker proviso compares others' situation with non-appropriation

Applies Nozick: since others are better off than in the unowned baseline, Mara's acquisition passes his proviso; Nozick himself says someone may not appropriate the only water hole in a desert and charge what he will, so even Nozick limits her
Labour-mixing objection: tomato juice; why does labour create ownership of the land rather than just of its products
Cohen's critique: the baseline of non-appropriation is too weak; alternatives such as joint ownership would be better for others; self-ownership and world ownership
Left-libertarian alternative: equal shares of natural resources; Mara owes compensation
Assesses whether the exchange is genuinely voluntary given the lack of alternatives (Marx/Cohen on compelled wage labour; republican domination)
Reasoned conclusion on Mara's entitlement
questions.modelAnswer:
Locke holds that each person owns her own labour, and by mixing it with unowned nature she makes it her property. Mara has fenced and irrigated land, so on this account she has some claim to it. But Locke's provisos limit her. Appropriation is legitimate only if enough, and as good, is left for others. When there is only one spring, nothing comparable remains. The spoilage proviso also suggests she cannot claim more than she can use without waste. In the First Treatise Locke also holds that a person in extreme need has a claim to another's surplus, which suggests that a monopoly on the means of survival cannot be used to extract labour on any terms. On Locke's view, then, her title is doubtful.

Nozick's entitlement theory holds that a distribution is just if holdings arose through just acquisition and transfer. His version of the Lockean proviso is weaker: an appropriation is legitimate unless it makes others worse off than they would be if the thing remained unowned. The settlers are better off working for Mara than scrambling for an unowned spring, so she appears to pass. Yet Nozick himself denies that someone may appropriate the only water hole in a desert and charge what he likes, and he says the proviso continues to restrict how an owner may use a monopoly. Even on his theory, Mara's freedom to set terms is limited.

Critics go further. Nozick's tomato juice example shows that mixing labour does not obviously confer ownership; it might simply waste the labour. Cohen argues that the baseline of 'no appropriation' is too weak. Other arrangements, such as joint ownership of the spring with Mara compensated for her improvements, would leave the settlers better off still, and Nozick gives no reason to prefer his baseline. Left-libertarians add that natural resources belong equally to all, so Mara owes the others for taking more than her share.

Finally, the exchange's voluntariness is questionable. The settlers can choose to work or go thirsty, which resembles Marx's worker, free to sell labour but in effect compelled to do so. Republicans would describe them as dominated by Mara.

Mara has a just claim to the value of her improvements, but not to exclusive control of the island's only spring. Locke's own provisos, Nozick's caveat about water holes and Cohen's critique all point to the same result.

questions.q: 'Rawls's theory of justice is silent on the injustices that most shape women's lives.' Discuss with reference to Okin and at least one other feminist critic.
markScheme: Rawls's basic structure includes the family in A Theory of Justice, but he treats the parties as heads of families and assumes family justice
Okin: gender is socially constructed; the gendered division of labour within families makes women vulnerable (economic dependence, vulnerability by marriage)
Okin: the family is the first school of moral development, so an unjust family undermines the sense of justice
Okin's constructive move: apply the original position with sex hidden; reforms like shared parenting, workplace changes, equal claims on household income
Rawls's later reply (Political Liberalism; 'The Idea of Public Reason Revisited'): family is part of the basic structure; principles constrain but do not directly regulate internal family life
Pateman: contract tradition itself rests on a sexual contract; Rawls cannot be fixed by inclusion
MacKinnon or Young: power and domination, not distribution; the 'distributive paradigm'
Evaluation: is the silence remediable within Rawls's framework (Okin's view) or symptomatic of a deeper problem (Pateman)?
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Rawls includes the family in the basic structure in A Theory of Justice, yet he says little about justice within it. The parties in the original position are described as heads of families, and the family appears mainly as the first school of moral development, assumed to be just.

Susan Moller Okin argues that this is a major omission. Gender, the social institutionalisation of sexual difference, structures nearly every aspect of life. The division of labour in which women do most unpaid care work makes them economically dependent, limits their opportunities, and leaves them vulnerable if the marriage ends. Since Rawls says the family is where children first learn justice, a family based on dominance and dependence teaches injustice. Okin's important point is that Rawls's own tools can be used against this: if the parties did not know their sex, they would choose institutions that shared paid and unpaid work equally, protected the economically dependent spouse, and supported both parents in caring.

Rawls replied in later work that the family is part of the basic structure and that the principles of justice constrain it, guaranteeing women's equal rights, but do not directly regulate its internal life, much as they do not govern churches or universities. Critics respond that this protects exactly the space in which much gender injustice occurs.

Other feminists argue that the problem is deeper. Carole Pateman claims that the social contract tradition depends on a prior sexual contract establishing men's right over women, and that the abstract 'individual' who contracts is implicitly male. On this view adding women to Rawls's framework cannot succeed, because contract has been a means of subordination. Iris Marion Young argues that a focus on distributing goods neglects domination and cultural imperialism, which shape women's lives beyond their share of resources.

The claim is partly correct. Rawls's original theory was largely silent on gender injustice in the family, as Okin showed. But Okin also demonstrates that the framework can be extended to address it. Whether this is sufficient depends on whether one sees gender injustice primarily as unfair distribution within institutions, which Rawls can address, or as a structure of domination embedded in the contract tradition, as Pateman argues.

questions.q: 'Liberal rights are bourgeois rights: they promise freedom and equality to all but deliver neither to the worker.' Assess this Marxist critique of liberal accounts of liberty and equality.
markScheme: Marx's 'On the Jewish Question': political emancipation vs human emancipation; rights of man as rights of egoistic, separated individuals; liberty as 'separation of man from man'
Capital: the worker is 'free' in a double sense, free to sell labour power and free from means of production; formal freedom masks compulsion and exploitation
Critique of the Gotha Programme: equal right is a right of inequality; 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'
Ideology: base and superstructure; liberal ideals legitimise class relations
Contemporary developments: Cohen on proletarian unfreedom and money; republican domination at work; Young's exploitation

Liberal replies: rights are not merely bourgeois; they protect workers too (association, unions, suffrage); Rawls's fair value of political liberty, fair equality of opportunity and difference principle respond to class inequality
Evaluation: formal vs substantive freedom; whether liberalism can absorb the critique or whether it requires abolishing private ownership of the means of production
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Marx's critique begins in 'On the Jewish Question' (1843). Political emancipation, the granting of equal civil and political rights, is real progress, but it is not human emancipation. The 'rights of man' are the rights of egoistic individuals separated from one another: liberty is the right to be left alone, property the right to use one's goods without regard to others. Political equality coexists with deep inequality in civil society, the sphere of work and property. In Capital, the worker is free in a double sense: legally free to sell his labour power, and 'free' of any means of production, so compelled in practice to sell it. Behind the equal exchange of wages for labour lies exploitation. In the Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875), even equal right, payment according to labour, is a right of inequality, because it ignores differing needs. Liberal ideals thus serve as ideology, presenting class relations as free and fair.

The critique has considerable force. Formal liberty to refuse a job means little if the alternative is destitution; Cohen shows that lack of money exposes people to interference, so poverty restricts even negative freedom. Republicans add that workers who depend on employers' discretion are dominated. Young lists exploitation, the transfer of the fruits of one group's labour to another, as a face of oppression that distributive theories may miss.

Liberals reply that rights are not merely bourgeois. Freedom of association made trade unions possible; universal suffrage gave workers political power; free expression enabled socialist movements. Modern egalitarian liberalism also absorbs much of the critique. Rawls guarantees the fair value of political liberty, requires fair equality of opportunity and permits inequality only when it benefits the least advantaged; in his later work he rejected welfare-state capitalism in favour of property-owning democracy or liberal socialism.

The Marxist may reply that while the means of production remain privately owned by a minority, these measures leave the basic relation of dependence intact. Whether that is decisive depends on empirical questions about how far reforms within liberal democracy can reduce workers' dependence.

The claim is overstated: liberal rights have delivered real freedoms to workers, and the critique itself relies on values of freedom and equality that liberals share. But it rightly shows that formal rights are not enough. A liberalism that ignores the material conditions of freedom leaves the worker formally equal but substantively unfree.

questions.q: 'The social contract tradition is not merely incomplete in its treatment of race and gender; it is a theory of domination.' Critically evaluate this claim with reference to Pateman, Mills and at least one defender of contract theory.
markScheme: Sets out the social contract tradition: Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Rawls; legitimacy through agreement of free and equal individuals
Pateman: the sexual contract; men's right over women established through the original pact and marriage; the 'individual' modelled on men
Mills: the racial contract among whites; non-whites as subpersons; Locke's treatment of 'waste' land in America, his involvement with the Carolina constitutions; epistemology of ignorance
Distinguishes descriptive (historical) from normative uses of contract: Mills argues the actual contract was racial, but uses contract as a critical tool
Difference between Pateman (contract inherently subordinating) and Mills (contract can be reclaimed; non-ideal theory, corrective justice)
Defence of contract theory: Rawls's veil hides race and sex; Okin's feminist Rawlsianism; contract as a test of justifiability rather than history
Problems with defence: ideal theory abstracts from oppression (Mills); hypothetical parties are idealised; Okin's evidence that 'neutral' theory overlooked gender
Intersectional considerations (Crenshaw): race and gender interacting, contract analyses may treat them separately
Sustained evaluation with a defended conclusion
Accurate use of thinkers and clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
Social contract theory holds that political authority is legitimate if free and equal individuals did, or would, agree to it. The claim under discussion argues that the tradition did not merely leave people out but actively served to justify their subordination.

Carole Pateman's The Sexual Contract (1988) argues that the original pact was also a sexual one, establishing men's political right over women. Pateman concludes that contract is not a neutral vehicle of freedom: the 'individual' it presupposes is modelled on men, so feminists cannot simply extend contract to women.

Charles Mills's The Racial Contract (1997) offers a parallel argument about race. The actual contract underlying modern European politics was among whites, who classed non-whites as subpersons excluded from its protections. Locke's treatment of uncultivated land as waste helped justify the seizure of Indigenous land, and he was involved in administering the Carolina colony, whose Fundamental Constitutions sanctioned slavery. It is sustained by an 'epistemology of ignorance'.

The two critics differ: Pateman is sceptical of contract as such; Mills treats it as a historical description of injustice but still uses contractarian reasoning as a critical tool. He argues for a non-ideal liberalism that starts from actual domination and asks what corrective justice requires.

Defenders reply that contract theory is a test of justification, not history. Rawls's veil of ignorance hides race and sex, so principles that subordinate any group would be rejected. Okin showed how this device can be turned against gender injustice. On this view the tradition's failures were failures to apply its own principles.

This defence has force but faces two problems. First, Mills argues that ideal theory's abstractions are not neutral: by idealising persons and assuming full compliance it leaves out precisely the facts of domination that a theory of justice most needs. Second, the tradition's leading figures did not merely overlook women and non-Europeans; they argued for their exclusion. Crenshaw's intersectionality also shows that treating race and gender as separate add-ons misses how they combine.

I conclude that the claim is true historically but not as a claim about the tradition's normative potential. The classical contract was used as a theory of domination. But Mills's own approach, and Okin's, show that contractarian reasoning about free and equal persons can be turned into a powerful critique of domination, provided it starts from non-ideal reality rather than idealised assumptions.
